principles.title: Pair every standard with purpose
principles.rule: Write the reason and the intended use next to every token group and component, not only its value.
principles.why: A value with no stated reason cannot settle an edge case and invites taste arguments.
principles.apply: In DESIGN.md give each color role, type style and component a use-when line before the system is handed on.
principles.test: Every token group and component entry in DESIGN.md has a non-empty purpose or use-when line.

principles.title: Extend the system, not exceptions
principles.rule: When a screen needs something the system lacks, add it to the system first and then use it, instead of styling a local exception.
principles.why: Local one-off styles are where design debt starts.
principles.apply: List each new style or component a deliverable introduces, then either add it to DESIGN.md and the tokens or log a written exception in design/decisions.md.
principles.test: Every style in the deliverable maps to a system entry or to a logged exception.

principles.title: Give each component one job
principles.rule: Describe each component's job in one sentence and split any component whose description needs a second job joined by and.
principles.why: A narrow component fits more contexts and costs less to change.
principles.apply: Write the one-sentence job before building the component; when a second clause appears, make two components.
principles.test: Each component doc states a single job in one sentence.

principles.title: Version the system as product
principles.rule: Give the design system a version number, a changelog and a named owner, and treat the first release as version one rather than the finish.
principles.why: Needs keep changing, so a system with no owner or history decays.
principles.apply: When a project grows a DESIGN.md, add a version line, an owner and a dated change list at the top.
principles.test: DESIGN.md or the token file carries a version, an owner and a changelog entry for its last change.

principles.title: Inventory before redesigning a product
principles.rule: Count the unique colors, type sizes, type families and spacing values of an existing product before proposing a system for it.
principles.why: The number of near-duplicates shows how much to merge and where.
principles.apply: Report the counts with a proposed reduced set; skip the count only when the brief says the product is new.
principles.test: An inventory lists current and target counts per attribute, or the brief states that the product does not exist yet.

principles.title: Board every variant, then merge
principles.rule: Collect one screenshot of every live variant of each interface element on a single board and mark each keep, merge or remove.
principles.why: Seeing all variants together exposes redundancy that no single screen shows.
principles.apply: Group the board by element kind and agree the keep, merge or remove marks with the user before tokens are written.
principles.test: Each element group on the board has a screenshot per variant and a decision per variant.

principles.title: Ask system users first
principles.rule: Before designing a system, ask the people who will build with it and the person who funds it what hurts today and how success will be measured.
principles.why: A system that fits real workflows gets used, and the funder's concern becomes the success metric.
principles.apply: Record who was asked, their top problems and at least one measurable goal in design/brief.md.
principles.test: The brief names the people consulted, their problems and one measurable goal for the system.

principles.title: Give every color one job
principles.rule: Assign each palette color one role, such as action, feedback, information or hierarchy, and never let one value carry two conflicting roles.
principles.why: Interface color carries meaning beyond brand expression, and a shared value confuses that meaning.
principles.apply: Name the role of each color token in DESIGN.md before using it in a layout.
principles.test: Every palette entry has exactly one stated role, and no value serves both a brand role and a status role.

principles.title: Grow the palette on demand
principles.rule: Start the palette from a few brand primaries, one interactive color, neutrals and state colors, and add a tint or shade only when a component needs it.
principles.why: Extra choices produce inconsistent use.
principles.apply: Default: three brand primaries at most. Remove any tint or shade no component uses.
principles.test: Each tint and shade in the palette is used by at least one component.

principles.title: Shift hue when shading colors
principles.rule: When darkening or lightening a hue turns it muddy, mix toward a neighboring hue instead of pure black or white.
principles.why: A yellow darkened with black reads as brown, while one darkened toward orange stays yellow.
principles.apply: Build each hue ramp, view it as a strip, and fix any step that leaves its hue family.
principles.test: Viewed side by side, no step of a hue ramp reads as a different hue family.

principles.title: Record contrast for every pairing
principles.rule: Measure and record the contrast of every text and background pair the palette allows, using the thresholds of the accessibility gate.
principles.why: A palette that fails some readers fails as a palette.
principles.apply: Write a contrast grid into DESIGN.md and recheck it whenever a color token changes.
principles.test: A contrast grid lists each allowed foreground and background pair with its ratio and a pass or fail mark.

principles.title: Never code categories by color alone
principles.rule: Pair every color-coded category or state with a label, icon, pattern or position.
principles.why: Readers with a color vision deficiency cannot separate categories that differ only in hue.
principles.apply: Add the second channel when the legend or status set is designed, not after review.
principles.test: Every color-coded category in the deliverable also carries a non-color cue.

principles.title: Load few families, justify weights
principles.rule: Use one text family plus a monospace where code appears, add a display face only with a written reason, and list every loaded weight with its purpose.
principles.why: Each family and weight costs load time and dilutes the voice.
principles.apply: Default: two families, three at most for a single brand. Record the reason for each extra face in DESIGN.md.
principles.test: The type spec lists every loaded family and weight with a reason for each.

principles.title: Thin weights only at display
principles.rule: Reserve thin and light weights for display sizes and keep any text below heading size at regular weight or heavier.
principles.why: Thin strokes lose legibility at small sizes.
principles.apply: Check each text style in the scale: if it is below heading size, set a regular or heavier weight.
principles.test: No text style smaller than the smallest heading uses a weight lighter than regular.

principles.title: Derive sizes from one scale
principles.rule: Derive every type size from one base size and one ratio, and list any size that falls off that scale.
principles.why: Proportional sizes relate to each other instead of to taste.
principles.apply: Default: a 16 px base, set as 1rem on the web. Pick the ratio from the brief's tone, then generate the steps.
principles.test: Each size token equals the base times the ratio to an integer power, within rounding, or is listed as an exception.

principles.title: Unitless leading, tighter for headings
principles.rule: Set line height as a unitless multiple, looser for body text and tighter for headings.
principles.why: Unitless values scale with the font, and large type needs less leading.
principles.apply: Default: 1.4 to 1.5 for body text and about 1.1 to 1.3 for headings.
principles.test: Line-height tokens carry no unit and the body value is larger than every heading value.

principles.title: Space on a four-based scale
principles.rule: Take every spacing and sizing value from one scale built on a base of four, and comment any off-scale value with its reason.
principles.why: Platform metrics, common icon sizes and the default text size all divide by four, so parts align.
principles.apply: Default: base 4. A documented compensation, such as subtracting a 1 px border, is the only allowed exception.
principles.test: Every spacing token is a multiple of the base, and each exception in the styles carries a comment.

principles.title: Let content set the size
principles.rule: Avoid fixed widths and heights so elements fill their container, and give images a maximum width with automatic height.
principles.why: Content-sized elements survive responsive layouts without overflow.
principles.apply: Before finalizing, resize the render from phone width to wide desktop and fix every clip or overflow.
principles.test: At phone width and wide desktop width nothing overflows or clips, and each fixed dimension in the styles has a reason.

principles.title: Write the icon spec first
principles.rule: Write the icon rules, meaning fill or outline, stroke weight, color count, sizes and live area, before drawing, and ship icons and illustrations as vector.
principles.why: Stated rules keep a set unified, and vectors scale cleanly.
principles.apply: Put the five answers in DESIGN.md; a separate style for navigation and utility icons is fine when each is defined.
principles.test: The icon spec answers all five questions and ten sampled icons match it.

principles.title: Tokenize the material layer
principles.rule: Give shadows, elevation, radii, borders and textures fixed token values, like color and type.
principles.why: These decorations shape hierarchy, so ad hoc values break it.
principles.apply: Define a short elevation and radius scale before styling surfaces.
principles.test: The distinct shadow and radius values in the artifact do not outnumber the tokens defined for them.

principles.title: Store every value as token
principles.rule: Keep every reusable color, size, space, radius and duration as a named token in one platform-neutral file, and reference only tokens in component styles.
principles.why: One store makes a global change a single edit and keeps platforms from drifting.
principles.apply: Generate platform variables from design/tokens.json instead of typing values into components.
principles.test: A scan of component styles finds no raw color, size or duration literal that a token covers.

principles.title: Theme by swapping values only
principles.rule: Build themes and sub-brands by changing token values over identical structure and markup.
principles.why: Brands can then share components, behavior and accessibility work while looking different.
principles.apply: Add a theme as a second value set in the token file; touch no component to make it work.
principles.test: Two themes differ only in token values; markup, class names and scripts are identical.

principles.title: Show every state as fixtures
principles.rule: Show each interactive component in every state it can take, including hover, focus, active, disabled and error, and reuse those examples as test fixtures.
principles.why: Static mocks omit states, and shared examples keep docs and tests in step.
principles.apply: Render a state sheet per component before handoff and point the tests at the same examples.
principles.test: For each interactive component the docs show every applicable state and the tests load those same examples.

principles.title: Build accessibility into components
principles.rule: Make each component keyboard operable, labelled and usable by a screen reader inside the system so every product inherits it.
principles.why: A fix made once in the system fixes every screen, and late fixes cost more.
principles.apply: Run keyboard-only use and an automated checker on each component example before it enters the system.
principles.test: Each component example works by keyboard alone and passes an automated accessibility check with zero errors.

principles.title: Breaking changes bump major
principles.rule: Version releases as major.minor.patch and bump the major number for any removed or renamed token, class or property.
principles.why: The number tells adopters how much to test.
principles.apply: Write a breaking-change definition and release notes with every published token or component change.
principles.test: Every release that removes or renames a token, class or property carries a major bump and notes.

principles.title: Deprecate with a path, never clone
principles.rule: Never fork a component under a new name to dodge a breaking change; deprecate it with a replacement, a migration note and a removal date.
principles.why: Clones with no deadline leave two versions to maintain forever.
principles.apply: When a component must change shape, write the migration note in the same edit as the change.
principles.test: No component name carries a numeric or new/old suffix, and each deprecated item has a replacement, a note and a date.

principles.title: Undocumented means outside the system
principles.rule: Treat any pattern missing from the documentation as outside the system, and keep the list of components in code identical to the list in the docs.
principles.why: Undocumented patterns get rebuilt as duplicates.
principles.apply: Compare the two lists at each finalize step and document or remove each mismatch.
principles.test: A diff of component names in code against component names in the docs is empty.

principles.title: Keep a candidates waiting room
principles.rule: Hold patterns that recur but are not yet in the system in a visible candidates list with where each is used and the decision pending.
principles.why: Popular patterns need a home before they are promoted.
principles.apply: Add a candidates section to DESIGN.md and review it at each project close.
principles.test: Each candidate lists where it is used and a pending decision.

source.part: Chapter 4: Putting your design system into practice

principles.title: Pilot on one real feature
principles.rule: Prove a new system on one real, self-contained feature, then review the system for bias toward that feature before generalizing it.
principles.why: A pilot shows real gaps, and an unreviewed pilot bakes one product's quirks into everything.
principles.apply: Without a pilot, start with the most painful part in its smallest form, such as spacing and type utilities, before components.
principles.test: The decision record names the pilot or the first incremental piece and a bias review after it.

source.part: Chapter 4: Putting your design system into practice

principles.title: Write a ranked priority line
principles.rule: Write one line that ranks the project's top qualities in order, such as clarity before elegance, so trade-offs resolve the same way every time.
principles.why: An explicit order settles conflicts that a list of equal values cannot.
principles.apply: Put the line at the top of design/brief.md and cite it whenever two good options pull apart.
principles.test: The brief holds a ranked priority line and later decisions that trade qualities cite it.

principles.title: Define voice by is and never
principles.rule: Define the writing voice with a few words for what it is now, what it aims to be and what it never is, and turn those words into per-channel copy rules.
principles.why: A never-list stops the voice from drifting into the category's default tone.
principles.apply: Capture hard-to-name qualities with a mood board or interviews before choosing the words.
principles.test: The voice section lists is, aims-to-be and never words, and each channel has at least one concrete rule derived from them.

principles.title: Design states and data, not pictures
principles.rule: Design at product fidelity, with real states, interactions and data, instead of one static picture of the ideal screen.
principles.why: A picture hides the empty, loading, error and crowded cases that decide whether a design works.
principles.apply: Before calling a screen designed, list its states and render at least the empty, error and longest-content cases.
principles.test: Each key screen has rendered empty, error and longest-content states, not only the ideal one.

source.part: Chapter 6: The future of design systems

principles.title: Give the design-code seam an owner
principles.rule: Name who owns the overlap between design and code for this project, with its concrete duties such as tokens, component docs and preview builds.
principles.why: Placing a designer next to a builder and hoping they collaborate fails as work scales.
principles.apply: In the handoff plan, assign the seam duties to the GDH, to the coding agent or to a named person, line by line.
principles.test: The handoff plan lists each seam duty with one owner.

principles.title: Answer the four product questions
principles.rule: Answer four questions for every piece of work: does it solve a real user problem, can users work it out, can it be built with the time and stack available, and does it help the business.
principles.why: A design that fails any one of the four fails as a product.
principles.apply: Put one line per question in design/brief.md and revisit them at each review.
principles.test: The brief or review note holds an explicit answer to each of the four questions.

principles.title: Separate fit from build quality
principles.rule: Give two separate verdicts on any deliverable: whether it is the right solution for the problem, and whether it is built well.
principles.why: A well-built wrong answer and a right answer built badly both fail, and one verdict hides the other.
principles.apply: Write the two verdicts as separate lines in every review and handoff note.
principles.test: Each review holds one verdict on problem fit and a separate verdict on build quality.

principles.title: Follow research over stakeholder taste
principles.rule: When research and a stakeholder's direction conflict, follow the evidence and say openly that you did.
principles.why: Stakeholders supply vision, but evidence shows what users need.
principles.apply: Log each departure from the stated direction in design/decisions.md with the evidence that caused it.
principles.test: Every decision that departs from stated direction cites its evidence in the decision record.

principles.title: Write a prototype purpose statement
principles.rule: Before building a prototype, write which problem it explores or validates, for which user, and the hypothesis it tests.
principles.why: A stated purpose scopes the prototype to one objective and stops gold-plating.
principles.apply: Put the statement at the top of the prototype file and reject work that does not serve it.
principles.test: The prototype header holds a filled purpose, user and hypothesis.

principles.title: Distrust the first solution
principles.rule: Treat the first solution as the weakest one and branch into alternatives before choosing.
principles.why: Effort spent on a first idea creates attachment that has nothing to do with its quality.
principles.apply: Produce at least one deliberately different branch from the first idea, and record why each dropped branch failed.
principles.test: At least two distinct directions exist before one is chosen, and each dropped one has a recorded reason.

principles.title: Carry forward from failed branches
principles.rule: When a direction fails, name the cause and carry what worked into the next version instead of discarding it whole.
principles.why: Building on partial successes makes iteration fast.
principles.apply: Add a carried-forward line to each rejected option in design/decisions.md.
principles.test: Each rejected direction has a cause of failure and a note on what carried forward.

principles.title: Raise fidelity with confidence
principles.rule: Match fidelity to confidence: sketch while many answers are possible, wireframe as they narrow, and code an interactive build only once the direction is agreed.
principles.why: Low fidelity keeps options open; early polish fakes certainty.
principles.apply: Label each artifact with its fidelity and the confidence it reflects, and move up one step only when the current step's question is answered.
principles.test: No coded and styled prototype exists for an idea that has no agreed direction.

principles.title: Pick the prototype by question
principles.rule: Choose the prototype kind by what you must learn: a clickable static build for structure and flow, real content for content questions, and code for interaction, motion and responsiveness.
principles.why: Each kind answers a different question cheaply.
principles.apply: Name the question in the purpose statement and check that the chosen kind can answer it.
principles.test: The purpose statement names a question and the prototype kind matches it.

principles.title: Layout in boxes before content
principles.rule: Validate layout and flow with box-level wireframes that only label the content type in each region before adding detailed content.
principles.why: Structure problems are invisible once styled content arrives.
principles.apply: Keep the box version of each key screen and get structure agreed on it first.
principles.test: A box-level version of each key screen exists and predates the detailed version.

principles.title: No placeholder copy at high fidelity
principles.rule: Use real or realistic copy in every high-fidelity artifact.
principles.why: Placeholder text hides length, tone and hierarchy problems.
principles.apply: Ask the user for real copy or draft it from the brief; mark any copy still to confirm.
principles.test: A search of the high-fidelity artifact finds no lorem ipsum or generic filler strings.

principles.title: Mock data in shared prototypes
principles.rule: Use mock data, not real personal data, in any prototype that others will see.
principles.why: Mock data is flexible and cannot leak private records.
principles.apply: Generate realistic but fictional names and values unless the user approves real data for one test.
principles.test: The shared prototype's data holds no real names, email addresses or account numbers without a recorded approval.

principles.title: Look at the data first
principles.rule: Explore the real data's range, variance and shape before choosing a chart.
principles.why: Charts designed around invented data can come out flat or broken on real values.
principles.apply: Write a short data profile in the design notes and let the chart choice refer to it.
principles.test: The design note states range, variance and shape, and the chart choice cites them.

principles.title: Test charts on hard data
principles.rule: Render every chart with real or realistic data, including a low-variance case, an empty case and an extreme case, before it ships.
principles.why: A chart that looks persuasive in a mockup can be flat for nearly every real user.
principles.apply: Keep one capture per case beside the chart spec.
principles.test: Captures exist for each chart with realistic, flat, empty and extreme data.

principles.title: Mark undecided regions as placeholders
principles.rule: Put a plain marked placeholder in any region of a prototype that is still undecided, and list it as an open question.
principles.why: A marked gap invites discussion, while a guess passes for a decision.
principles.apply: Use a labelled box or static image for the region and copy the question into the open-questions list.
principles.test: Every undecided region is visibly marked and appears in the open-questions list.

principles.title: Spike risky parts early
principles.rule: Build a small working spike for any element with unclear feasibility, such as heavy motion, 3D, live data or a new interaction, before promising it.
principles.why: Feasibility is often unknown until the build starts.
principles.apply: Flag risky elements in the brief and schedule their spikes before visual polish.
principles.test: Each element flagged as risky has a working spike dated before the commitment.

principles.title: Design and build in handshake
principles.rule: Run design and build in parallel with repeated sync points instead of a single transfer at the end.
principles.why: Parallel work exposes edge cases that only the build reveals, while design can still absorb them.
principles.apply: Hand the coding agent an updated prototype each cycle and fold its edge-case reports into the next round.
principles.test: The project log shows more than one design-to-build sync point before delivery.

principles.title: Write outcomes per user type
principles.rule: Write the intended outcome for each type of user, tied to a pain point, and report each with a measured value after launch.
principles.why: Different users succeed in different ways, and a blended goal hides who is failing.
principles.apply: Add one outcome row per user type to the brief, and a before and after snapshot plan.
principles.test: The success list has one row per user type, each linked to a pain point.

principles.title: Agree the shared vocabulary
principles.rule: Agree a glossary so that design files and code use the same name for the same thing.
principles.why: Mismatched words such as component or layout cost hours of misunderstanding.
principles.apply: Add new terms to the glossary in DESIGN.md as they appear and use them in token and component names.
principles.test: Five sampled terms have the same name and meaning in the design files and in the code.

principles.title: Write a new-or-reuse test
principles.rule: Write down when a need justifies a new component and when it must reuse an existing one, and cite that test for every new component.
principles.why: An agreed test settles the most common design-system dispute before it starts.
principles.apply: Search the project and library before creating a component and record the result.
principles.test: Every new component in a change cites the new-or-reuse test and the search result.

principles.title: Turn repeat fixes into rules
principles.rule: When the same correction happens twice, add a rule, check or shared component so a third manual correction is not needed.
principles.why: Vigilance by one person is not a strategy; a system is.
principles.apply: Note repeated review comments and convert each into a token, a lint rule or a DESIGN.md rule.
principles.test: No correction appears three times in the review log without a matching rule or component.

principles.title: Refuse with an alternative
principles.rule: When declining a request on feasibility or quality grounds, state the constraint and offer at least one workable alternative.
principles.why: A flat no blocks collaboration between people with different mental models.
principles.apply: Phrase every refusal as constraint, consequence and one option the user can choose.
principles.test: Each refusal in the session names the constraint and gives at least one alternative.

principles.title: Learn constraints before proposing
principles.rule: As an outsider to a product, collect its technical and operational constraints by asking before you assume them.
principles.why: Broad generalists move fast but miss the inner limits a product team knows.
principles.apply: List the unknown constraints at intake and ask the user or the codebase owner about each.
principles.test: The brief marks each constraint as stated, found in the project or assumed.

principles.title: Name the quality bars explicitly
principles.rule: Report accessibility, responsiveness, performance and internationalization as separate lines in every UI review, even when the brief does not ask.
principles.why: Unprompted attention to these bars is what marks complete work.
principles.apply: Take thresholds from the accessibility gate and the discipline skill; this book names the bars, not the numbers.
principles.test: The review record holds one result line per bar.

principles.title: Label prototype or production
principles.rule: Label every code artifact as prototype or production, and never ship prototype code without passing the production checks.
principles.why: Validation and implementation have different goals and different quality bars.
principles.apply: Put the label in the file header and in the handoff note.
principles.test: Every delivered code file carries a prototype or production label.

principles.title: One edit changes one value
principles.rule: Build prototypes so that changing one design value, such as a speed, color, size or line of copy, takes one edit in one place.
principles.why: Validation work needs fast change for each feedback round.
principles.apply: Drive prototypes from the token file and a single content file.
principles.test: Changing one sampled value in the prototype takes exactly one edit.

principles.title: State cuts made for speed
principles.rule: When a deadline forces a cut, list what was cut and the quality it costs instead of trading quality away silently.
principles.why: Unspoken trade-offs cause the friction between design and build.
principles.apply: Add a cuts section to the handoff note with the user's acceptance of each cut.
principles.test: Every cut made for time appears in the handoff with its cost.

principles.title: Extract a reusable tool afterward
principles.rule: After solving a task, extract the component, script, template or rule that would solve it next time, or record why not.
principles.why: Design engineering aims at solutions that work now and again later.
principles.apply: Close each project with one reuse line in the retrospective.
principles.test: The project close note names an extracted reusable item or a reason for none.

principles.title: Fit the process to the need
principles.rule: When a step of the process does not fit the task, say so, adapt or skip it, and record the reason.
principles.why: The discipline's value is flexibility, not ritual.
principles.apply: Write skipped steps and their reasons into the decision record.
principles.test: Each skipped or adapted step has a recorded reason.

principles.title: Every animation needs a purpose
principles.rule: Give each animation one stated purpose, such as showing a state change, cause and effect, where something went, attention, feedback, a hidden affordance or brand emotion, and cut any with none.
principles.why: Motion that explains nothing spends the viewer's attention for no return.
principles.apply: Add a purpose column to the motion spec and delete rows whose purpose is only that it looks nice.
principles.test: Every row of the motion spec has a purpose from the allowed list.

principles.title: Animate changes people would miss
principles.rule: Add an in-between state to any change that would otherwise happen instantly and leave people unsure what changed.
principles.why: Software changes state faster than people can perceive.
principles.apply: List the appear, disappear, expand, load and value-change events of a flow and give each a transition or a written reason to stay instant.
principles.test: Each listed state change has a transition or a recorded reason for none.

principles.title: Show origin and destination
principles.rule: When an object enters or leaves because of a user action, move it from where it came from or to where it now lives.
principles.why: The path teaches the layout and links the action to its result.
principles.apply: For each such element, name its origin or resting place in the motion spec before choosing the move.
principles.test: After one viewing, a reviewer can name where each entering or leaving element came from or went.

principles.title: Motion never carries meaning alone
principles.rule: Give every meaningful visual change a non-visual equivalent, such as an announcement, a state attribute or an accessibility label.
principles.why: People who cannot rely on sight get nothing from a change that exists only as movement.
principles.apply: When a field shakes on error, also set its error state in markup or a hint string; keep warnings and legal statements as text.
principles.test: The number of meaningful animations equals the number of matching non-visual signals in the code.

principles.title: Primary actions never hide
principles.rule: Keep core controls visible at rest and use motion only to hint at secondary features that are tucked away.
principles.why: Hints invite discovery, but primary tasks must not depend on discovery.
principles.apply: Check each screen with all animation paused: every primary action must still be visible.
principles.test: With motion paused, every primary action of each screen is visible.

principles.title: Push back at limits
principles.rule: Make a control that cannot go further respond with gentle resistance and return, instead of doing nothing.
principles.why: Feedback proportional to input tells people a limit exists and invites them to adjust.
principles.apply: Drag, press or scroll past each limit in the prototype and design the response.
principles.test: No tested limit is a silent dead end.

principles.title: Match motion to product temperament
principles.rule: Choose motion character from the brand's emotional tone: springier for playful, fast and tight for precise tools, slow and even for calm.
principles.why: Motion sets mood as strongly as color and type.
principles.apply: Put two or three motion adjectives in the brief and tune easing and amplitude to them.
principles.test: A reviewer who watches the prototype without the brief picks adjectives that overlap the brief's motion adjectives.

principles.title: Ration expressive motion
principles.rule: Reserve large expressive animation for a few named moments in the journey, such as finishing a big task, and keep everything else functional.
principles.why: Expressive bursts carry feeling that words cannot, and lose force when used everywhere.
principles.apply: Tag each animation functional or expressive and map each expressive one to a journey moment.
principles.test: No screen runs more than one expressive animation at once, and each expressive one maps to a named moment.

principles.title: Perceptible duration for meaning
principles.rule: Give any transition meant to be seen enough time to register, and allow shorter times only for press feedback.
principles.why: Below the perception floor a change reads as a jump and its context is lost.
principles.apply: Default: at least 100 ms of visible movement for motion that carries meaning. Brand tokens set longer page and flourish timings.
principles.test: No meaningful transition in the tokens or code is shorter than the stated floor.

principles.title: Several durations, not one
principles.rule: Use a small duration scale with different steps for view changes, small state changes and loaders, and lengthen each only as much as it needs.
principles.why: One timing everywhere ignores what each transition must carry.
principles.apply: Map each duration token to a role: control, surface, page or flourish.
principles.test: The duration scale has more than one step and each token names its role.

principles.title: No linear easing on movement
principles.rule: Never move an object at constant speed; give movement acceleration and deceleration.
principles.why: Uniform speed does not exist in the physical world, so it looks mechanical.
principles.apply: Allow linear timing only for continuous loops such as spinners and progress bars.
principles.test: No transform or position animation uses linear timing except a continuous loop.

principles.title: Ease out in, ease in out
principles.rule: Default to decelerating curves for elements that enter or gain attention and accelerating curves for elements that leave or lose it.
principles.why: An arriving object should land and settle; a departing one should gather speed.
principles.apply: Map each animation's direction to an easing token and adjust only after testing by feel.
principles.test: Each enter animation uses an ease-out token and each exit an ease-in token, or a logged exception.

principles.title: Name the physical analog
principles.rule: Choose any non-default easing by naming the real object it imitates, such as a drawer, a door or a sheet of paper.
principles.why: Familiar physics makes a digital object believable.
principles.apply: Write the analog in the motion spec row; with no analog, use the default token.
principles.test: Every non-default easing in the spec names its analog.

principles.title: Springs barely seen, scoped
principles.rule: Keep overshoot at the edge of perception and use springs only where the design system allows them, or, with no system, on gesture-driven or interruptible movement.
principles.why: Noticed bounce distracts and breaks a calm or precise tone.
principles.apply: Use plain easing for opacity and color; reserve follow-through for position, scale and rotation of prominent elements.
principles.test: A first-time viewer does not describe any element as bouncing, and no spring is applied to opacity or color.

principles.title: Stage before swapping in place
principles.rule: Before replacing content in place, such as a caption or status, add a brief out phase or pause so the viewer notices the change.
principles.why: A hard swap is easy to miss when the eye is elsewhere.
principles.apply: Use the out phase for text and value regions that update while the user looks at something else.
principles.test: No in-place content replacement is a hard cut.

principles.title: Numbers move with their direction
principles.rule: Animate a changing number upward when it rises and downward when it falls, instead of only flashing it.
principles.why: Direction tells the viewer what the value did without comparing from memory.
principles.apply: Apply it to live metrics and counters; the final value must land exact and stable.
principles.test: Raising and then lowering a metric produces two opposite motions and an exact final value.

principles.title: Secondary motion stays secondary
principles.rule: Keep supporting motion weaker than the primary motion so it adds nuance without drawing the eye.
principles.why: Secondary motion is punctuation; when it competes it reverses the hierarchy.
principles.apply: Use secondary action to signal a threshold, such as a swipe turning destructive, before release.
principles.test: A first-time viewer names the primary element first when asked what moved.

principles.title: Stagger groups, cap the total
principles.rule: Offset the start of similar items entering together, shrink the gap between successive items, and keep the total cascade time capped at any item count.
principles.why: A fixed step that suits three items drags at twelve.
principles.apply: Default: test the cascade at 1, 3, 12 and 20 items. A decaying delay, such as a square root curve, keeps it tight.
principles.test: Per-item delay is above zero, the gaps shrink, and the total time stays within the project cap at every tested count.

principles.title: Choose signature motions
principles.rule: Define a small set of signature motions that carry the brand and state where each may appear.
principles.why: Appeal is the animated form of branding, and an unbounded signature becomes noise.
principles.apply: Design one or two signature moves during exploration, tied to the brand's subject rather than to a stock effect.
principles.test: The motion section names its signature motions with allowed places, and each appears only there.

principles.title: Plan motion at wireframe stage
principles.rule: Write motion notes, meaning what moves, from where and why, into the first layout deliverable instead of adding motion after the build.
principles.why: Late motion feels bolted on and leaves no time for accessibility testing.
principles.apply: Annotate wireframes with motion intent the moment a flow is drawn.
principles.test: The first layout deliverable contains motion notes.

principles.title: Spec motion in four blocks
principles.rule: Describe every animation with the same four fields: behavior, easing, duration and sequencing.
principles.why: One shared vocabulary lets design and build talk about the same motion.
principles.apply: Use the four fields plus purpose as the columns of the motion spec handed to code.
principles.test: Every row of the motion spec has behavior, easing, duration and sequencing filled.

principles.title: One environment statement
principles.rule: State the single feeling every detail must support, such as calm and unhurried, and reject motion that breaks it.
principles.why: One explicit target gives a yes or no test for each animation.
principles.apply: Write the statement after research, put it in the brief, and ask of each animation whether it supports it.
principles.test: The brief holds one environment statement and each motion review records a yes or no against it.

principles.title: Tune timing in a sandbox
principles.rule: Tune timing in a standalone prototype with adjustable variables, and ship the exact values signed off there.
principles.why: Fast iteration finds the right feel; production code is slow to change.
principles.apply: Expose duration and easing as controls in the prototype and copy the approved values into tokens.
principles.test: Production motion values equal the values recorded at prototype sign-off.

principles.title: Motion is a system section
principles.rule: Keep motion principles, duration and easing tokens, guidance per interaction type and examples together in one section of the design system.
principles.why: Without one source, teams duplicate work and the product feels inconsistent.
principles.apply: Cover feedback, hints, hierarchy, relationships and navigation, each with a do and a do-not example.
principles.test: The design system has a motion section with principles, tokens and guidance per interaction type.

principles.title: Bake motion into components
principles.rule: Build curves and durations into shared components so feature work never picks timing per instance.
principles.why: Teams can then assemble screens knowing motion is already right and on brand.
principles.apply: Log each per-instance override as an exception that ends in a new token or a rejection.
principles.test: Feature code holds no per-instance duration or easing override without a logged exception.

principles.title: Message stays long enough
principles.rule: Give every auto-dismissing animated message a minimum display time long enough for a reader and a screen reader to finish it.
principles.why: A toast that leaves too fast is lost, most of all to assistive technology.
principles.apply: Set the minimum as a token and test it with a screen reader; this book gives no value.
principles.test: Each auto-dismissing element has a documented minimum time and is fully read by a screen reader before removal.

principles.title: Gestures need a labelled alternative
principles.rule: Give every gesture-only action a focusable, labelled control or an accessibility action that does the same thing.
principles.why: A gesture taught by animation is undiscoverable without sight or fine motor control.
principles.apply: List gestures in the spec with their alternative route beside each.
principles.test: Every gesture-triggered action is reachable through a labelled control.

principles.title: Reduce until nearly unseen
principles.rule: Shrink each animation's amplitude, duration and number of moving parts until it stops communicating, then step back one notch.
principles.why: Motion should add value without stealing attention from the task.
principles.apply: Run this pass on every screen before finalizing and record the answer per animation.
principles.test: Critique notes record a reduction check for each animation.

principles.title: Connect states through shared elements
principles.rule: Animate the content two states share, such as the tapped card growing into its detail view, instead of sliding in an unrelated screen.
principles.why: Shared-element continuity keeps the tapped item visibly tied to the view it opens.
principles.apply: For each list-to-detail transition, name the shared elements and move them continuously.
principles.test: No list-to-detail transition uses a generic push when shared elements exist.

principles.title: Test motion in the worst case
principles.rule: Judge each animation at the largest realistic data volume and in the lowest-attention situation the users face.
principles.why: Motion that is fine in a demo can distract or endanger in real use.
principles.apply: Render the longest list or the busiest map and replay it as a glancing user would.
principles.test: Each animation has a recorded pass or fail at maximum realistic data and in the lowest-attention scenario.

principles.title: Look alike, respond alike
principles.rule: Give elements that look alike the same class of response to the same input, and give a member that cannot act a soft response in the same physical language.
principles.why: A mismatch between expectation and response breaks trust.
principles.apply: Group components by look and test one input across each group.
principles.test: Within each visual group the same input produces the same class of response, and no member is inert.

principles.title: Gestures track and reverse
principles.rule: Make gesture-driven motion follow the input continuously and let the user reverse or cancel it halfway.
principles.why: Fluid interfaces act while the user is still deciding.
principles.apply: Prototype gestures in code, not only on a timeline, with design and build tuning together.
principles.test: Reversing a drag halfway returns the element smoothly with no jump or forced completion.

principles.title: Borrow methods from other fields
principles.rule: When the usual design method stalls, borrow a working method from a field outside design, such as improv, science or comedy writing, and name where it came from.
principles.why: The book's premise is that design teams learn from every discipline and that cross-field methods raise a team's output.
principles.apply: During exploration, pick one outside practice as a deliberate lens and note it in the decision record.
principles.test: The exploration notes name at least one method or reference from outside the project's own field.

principles.title: Restate their view first
principles.rule: Before disagreeing with a user preference, restate their view accurately in their own terms, then offer your option.
principles.why: Design only lands when you meet people where they are.
principles.apply: Open each disagreement in the chat with a one-line restatement of what the user wants and why.
principles.test: Each disagreement reply opens with an accurate restatement of the user's position.

principles.title: Hand off the why
principles.rule: Put the goal, audience and constraint behind a task into every handoff and sub-agent prompt, and leave the how open where you can.
principles.why: Explaining why lets the receiver find a better solution; dictating how removes that chance.
principles.apply: Add a why-this-matters line to each delegation and each handoff note.
principles.test: Every handoff note and delegation prompt holds a why-this-matters line.

principles.title: Ask what they mean
principles.rule: Meet a surprising or unclear idea during creation with a clarifying question instead of a judgment.
principles.why: A question exposes a mismatch without shutting the idea down.
principles.apply: In explore rounds, ask what the user means before replying with any objection.
principles.test: No reply in an explore round rejects an idea before a clarifying question about it.

principles.title: Build on their idea
principles.rule: In each new iteration, keep or extend at least one element the user proposed and name it.
principles.why: Partners reach places neither reaches alone, even through a misunderstanding.
principles.apply: After feedback, start the next round from the user's contribution, then add yours.
principles.test: Each iteration after feedback names at least one user-proposed element it keeps or extends.

principles.title: No hidden favorite
principles.rule: Present options with equal care and detail, and label your recommendation separately from the descriptions.
principles.why: People spot a steered choice at once, and it kills honest feedback.
principles.apply: Describe what each option does in the same format, then add a labelled recommendation block.
principles.test: Option descriptions have parallel structure and the recommendation sits in its own labelled block.

principles.title: Provoke when a round stalls
principles.rule: When a round produces no directional feedback, add one clearly labelled provocation that breaks a stated assumption of the brief.
principles.why: Some tension is needed for people to push past the safe answer.
principles.apply: Pick the assumption most taken for granted, invert it, and show the result beside the safe options.
principles.test: After a round with no directional feedback, the next round contains one labelled provocation option.

principles.title: Know the collaborator's goal
principles.rule: At kickoff, learn who you are working with, what they are trying to achieve and which metric they answer to, then design toward the overlap with the design goal.
principles.why: Shared goals build trust and let each party then work independently.
principles.apply: Record the user's role, goal and metric in the brief and name one design decision that serves it.
principles.test: The brief names the collaborator's metric and at least one design decision that serves it.

principles.title: Agree who owns what
principles.rule: Before work starts, list what the agent decides, what the user decides and what belongs to others such as copy, engineering or legal.
principles.why: Claiming the whole product makes everyone else subordinate and damages the work.
principles.apply: Use the role list to assign an owner to each later decision in design/decisions.md.
principles.test: Every decision in the record has an owner taken from the agreed role list.

principles.title: Draw from distant references
principles.rule: Build each reference set from at least three distinct domains or styles, and keep dissenting views in the record instead of deleting them.
principles.why: New ideas come from overlaying unlike sources, and sameness finds fewer insights.
principles.apply: Default: three source domains per board, at least one outside the project's category.
principles.test: The board or option set draws on three or more distinct domains and the record keeps minority views.

principles.title: Mirror the real audience
principles.rule: Check that imagery, names, sample data and copy reflect the documented audience rather than the people making the work.
principles.why: Makers are never the core users, and their defaults leak into the design.
principles.apply: Compare each human and content element against the audience in the brief and list mismatches.
principles.test: A review lists the deliverable's people, names and sample data against the documented audience with mismatches noted.

principles.title: Ask the worst case
principles.rule: At kickoff, ask what the worst outcome of the design could be and for whom, and give each risk a mitigation or an explicit acceptance.
principles.why: Good intent does not guarantee good impact.
principles.apply: Add a risk list naming at least two affected groups to design/brief.md.
principles.test: The brief has a worst-case list with affected groups and a mitigation or acceptance for each.

principles.title: Trust what people do
principles.rule: Tag every piece of feedback as observed or stated, and follow observed behavior when the two conflict.
principles.why: What people say they want often differs from what they choose.
principles.apply: Show options and watch which one the user picks or uses, instead of only asking whether they like it.
principles.test: Feedback items carry an observed or stated tag and conflicts follow the observed item.

principles.title: Ask about the artifact in view
principles.rule: Ask questions about the artifact in front of the person, not about hypotheticals or memory.
principles.why: Out of context, people fill gaps with plausible answers that do not match their behavior.
principles.apply: Phrase review questions as tasks on the screen, such as finding a control, not as would-you-use questions.
principles.test: Review questions refer to the shown artifact, with none asking for prediction or recall.

principles.title: Pair numbers with reasons
principles.rule: Back any data-justified decision with both a behavioral number and an observed reason, or state which one is missing.
principles.why: A number alone can mean interest or confusion.
principles.apply: Write the what and the why on the same line in the decision record.
principles.test: Each data-backed decision cites a number and a reason, or names the missing half.

principles.title: Write a three-line POV
principles.rule: Write a point of view for each project with three labelled lines: the specific person served, their deep unmet need, and why that is a real insight.
principles.why: It gives the design an emotional benchmark beyond countable metrics.
principles.apply: Make the person line concrete and the need a verb phrase, not a feature.
principles.test: The brief holds User, Need and Insight lines, and the need line names no feature.

principles.title: Success means do and feel
principles.rule: Define success with at least one measure of what people do and one target for what they should feel.
principles.why: Teams measure behavior well and forget the feeling, which matters just as much.
principles.apply: Phrase the feeling target so a reviewer can observe it, such as visible relief at checkout.
principles.test: The success criteria hold at least one behavior measure and one feeling target.

principles.title: Mission is now, vision is later
principles.rule: Keep a present-tense mission of what the work does now and why separate from a future-tense vision of where it is going.
principles.why: The two do different jobs and blur when merged.
principles.apply: Check each deliverable against the mission with a plain yes or no and one sentence of evidence.
principles.test: The brand docs hold two distinct statements, and each review records a mission yes or no with evidence.

principles.title: Tell the design's story
principles.rule: Give every presented concept a two or three sentence story of what it is and why someone would use it.
principles.why: People adopt and spread what they can explain.
principles.apply: Write the story before the visuals and check that a non-designer can repeat it back.
principles.test: Each presented concept carries a short story that a non-designer can restate.

principles.title: Diverge before converging
principles.rule: Label each phase diverge or converge, and run a diverge phase before any single direction is refined on an open-ended request.
principles.why: Analytical narrowing on an ill-defined problem wastes time and kills ideas.
principles.apply: For a new brand, look or product, show the diverge output before polishing one option.
principles.test: The plan labels each phase, and an open-ended project shows a diverge phase before refinement.

principles.title: Defer the decision
principles.rule: Explore materials and options for longer and commit to a composition later than feels comfortable.
principles.why: More creative makers play longer and decide later.
principles.apply: Default: three materially different directions exist before one is chosen, and the record shows the choice came after them.
principles.test: The decision record dates the choice after three or more materially different directions.

source.part: Chapter 6: Creativity, innovation, and divergent thinking

principles.title: Draft your own first
principles.rule: Draft your own options before you judge someone else's references or assets.
principles.why: A few minutes of original ideation makes people more open to novel ideas when screening.
principles.apply: When the user brings a reference, sketch alternatives first, then review the reference against them.
principles.test: In reviews of outside references, the log shows the agent's own alternatives drafted first.

source.part: Chapter 6: Creativity, innovation, and divergent thinking

principles.title: Generate options independently
principles.rule: Produce early options in separate passes that do not see each other, under a fixed time or count budget, before any comparison.
principles.why: Parallel silent work keeps the loudest voice, or the first draft, from setting the direction.
principles.apply: Default: eight small rough options, invite the user to add theirs before seeing yours.
principles.test: Early options were generated independently and their count matches the stated budget.

source.part: Chapter 6: Creativity, innovation, and divergent thinking

principles.title: Vote in named categories
principles.rule: Converge by picking a winner in named categories such as easiest win, most delightful and moon shot, rather than one overall favorite.
principles.why: Categories keep a bold option alive next to the safe ones.
principles.apply: Carry at least one bold option forward or record why it was dropped.
principles.test: The shortlist shows each pick with its category and the fate of the boldest option.

source.part: Chapter 6: Creativity, innovation, and divergent thinking

principles.title: Every option gets a hearing
principles.rule: Give each option one recorded strength and one recorded concern before choosing.
principles.why: Skipping options biases the pick toward the first one shown.
principles.apply: Write the strength and concern lines as you present, not after the choice.
principles.test: The review record holds a strength and a concern for every option.
