principles.title: Write the brief first
principles.rule: Write a short prose brief that states the change the work should make and for whom before making any visual.
principles.why: Words are the one format every discipline can read and they keep the work on track.
principles.apply: Do not start visuals until the user confirms or edits the brief.
principles.test: A confirmed brief file exists and predates the first visual.

principles.title: Make the brief deniable
principles.rule: Write at least three this-not-that statements into the brief, and strike any sentence that would be true for every project.
principles.why: A brief nobody could disagree with says nothing.
principles.apply: Pair each brand word with what it rules out, such as calm not sleepy.
principles.test: The brief holds three or more explicit exclusions, and no sentence is generic enough to fit any project.

principles.title: Describe the feel first
principles.rule: Describe how the result should feel in use, in sensory words, before choosing any visual.
principles.why: Prose carries warmth, pace and atmosphere without fixing a layout too early.
principles.apply: Write one paragraph with no layout or component words and use it to judge directions.
principles.test: The brief contains a sensory paragraph free of layout or component vocabulary.

principles.title: Prototype the biggest risk
principles.rule: Point each prototype at one named question about the largest risk, rated as value, usability, feasibility or viability.
principles.why: The cheapest prototype that answers the riskiest question saves the most work.
principles.apply: Write a four-row risk table, pick the top row and build only enough to answer it.
principles.test: Each prototype names its question and its risk type.

principles.title: Fidelity follows the audience
principles.rule: Keep artifacts rough inside the working conversation and raise fidelity for viewers outside it.
principles.why: Makers read sketches fast, while outsiders need enough realism to grasp intent without narration.
principles.apply: Before sharing beyond the user, remove the explanation and check that the viewer can still state the purpose.
principles.test: An artifact for an outside viewer can be understood without a verbal walkthrough.

principles.title: Build both to end debates
principles.rule: When two positions on a direction persist, build cheap versions of both and compare them instead of arguing.
principles.why: A comparison artifact settles in minutes what a debate cannot.
principles.apply: Keep everything but the disputed variable equal.
principles.test: Disagreements that lasted more than one exchange end in a recorded comparison, not a prose thread.

principles.title: Label evidence and assumptions
principles.rule: List the evidence behind each major design decision, such as audience, primary task and feature set, and label every decision without evidence as an assumption.
principles.why: Designs built on guesses fail often and cost the most to fix.
principles.apply: Add an evidence list to design/brief.md that points each decision to data, an interview, a support theme or the user's own statement.
principles.test: Every key decision in the brief points to an evidence item or carries the label assumption.

principles.title: Mine existing data first
principles.rule: Ask for and read the data that already exists, such as analytics, support themes, sales notes and survey results, before asking for new research.
principles.why: Other teams often already hold the insight.
principles.apply: Record found or none available for each source type in the brief.
principles.test: The brief lists each existing-data source type with found or none available.

principles.title: Use the users' own words
principles.rule: Collect the words users use for the product and their tasks, and use those words in labels, headings and calls to action.
principles.why: Internal jargon hides the path users already think in.
principles.apply: Keep a short user-language list in the brief, taken from interviews, reviews or support messages.
principles.test: Labels and headings in the deliverable use terms from the user-language list, not internal names.

principles.title: Ask why people switch
principles.rule: For a redesign, find out why people adopt or abandon the product and decide whether the problem is function or perception.
principles.why: Users can leave a capable product because its simplicity reads as unsophisticated, which only interviews reveal.
principles.apply: Ask the user for switch interviews, exit answers or churn notes, and state function or perception in the brief.
principles.test: A redesign brief names its why-people-switch source and calls the problem function or perception.

principles.title: Keep a feedback channel running
principles.rule: Name one feedback source that keeps running after launch and where its results land.
principles.why: A standing signal gives fresh insight without new effort each time.
principles.apply: Add the channel, such as a post-signup question or a tagged feedback inbox, to the handoff note.
principles.test: The handoff names one continuous feedback source and its destination.

principles.title: Write the product story first
principles.rule: Write a short story of how the product fits into one person's life before designing any screen.
principles.why: A roadmap says what and when; a story says why, and people remember stories.
principles.apply: Draft the story with a setting, a routine, a change, two consequences and an outcome, and set it slightly in the future.
principles.test: A dated story exists before the first layout and answers how the product fits a person's life.

principles.title: Keep interface out of stories
principles.rule: Keep screens, components and technology out of the product story and describe only people, context, need and value.
principles.why: Interface detail in the story dictates the solution before exploration starts.
principles.apply: Strike any sentence that names a layout, component or required technology.
principles.test: The story artifact contains no layout, component or technology names.

principles.title: Ground stories in research
principles.rule: Base every character and plot point in the story on a research item or a user statement, and mark invented ones as assumptions.
principles.why: Stories that start from research point the team at real frustrations and hopes.
principles.apply: Link each plot point to its source in a footnote of the story.
principles.test: Each character and plot point links to a source or carries the label assumption.

principles.title: Shape journeys as story arcs
principles.rule: Lay a user journey on a story arc from setup and trigger through rising trouble, crisis and climax to resolution, with the user's words at each stage.
principles.why: An arc gives the map a clear problem, obstacles and payoff to design for.
principles.apply: Mark goals, hurdles, devices and channels at each stage.
principles.test: The journey map has the arc stages in order, each with a thought or quote and its hurdles and channels.

principles.title: Storyboard the user's feelings
principles.rule: Draw each storyboard panel with its setting, the action and the user's feeling at that step.
principles.why: Drawing forces decisions and puts emotion on every step.
principles.apply: Use rough panels; stick figures and photos are enough.
principles.test: Every storyboard panel states setting, action and feeling.

principles.title: Gate video stories by scope
principles.rule: Produce a video story only for a new product, a long project or a cross-channel experience, and keep detailed interface out of its script.
principles.why: Video is immersive but costly, so smaller scopes take a cheaper form.
principles.apply: Treat this as the check before any paid video generation for a vision piece.
principles.test: The plan records which of the three conditions justifies a vision video before one is made.

principles.title: Write job stories in context
principles.rule: Write each need as a job story: when a situation occurs, the person wants a motivation, so they can reach an outcome.
principles.why: A job story keeps the motive tied to its context, unlike a trait-based persona.
principles.apply: Draw each job story from a real statement and compare several to find patterns.
principles.test: Each job story has all three parts and cites the statement it came from.

principles.title: Explore at the lowest fidelity
principles.rule: Explore with text outlines, flow lists, grey boxes, thumbnails and rough palettes before producing any polished output.
principles.why: Polish looks certain, is hard to abandon and narrows exploration to a few ideas.
principles.apply: Do not generate hero images or styled components until a low-fidelity round has been reviewed.
principles.test: The log shows a reviewed low-fidelity step before the first high-fidelity artifact.

principles.title: Many rough concepts, then narrow
principles.rule: Generate many rough concepts that differ in structure or approach, not only in color or font, before selecting the directions to develop.
principles.why: Starting wide and narrowing finds ideas that a single polished pass never reaches.
principles.apply: Default: six to eight rough concepts at sketch level, narrowed to the kit's three directions.
principles.test: At least the stated number of structurally distinct rough concepts exists before selection.

principles.title: Limit the tool, not the idea
principles.rule: Set a hard limit on each exploration round, such as greyscale only, a fixed time or a fixed element count, so detail cannot creep in.
principles.why: Fine tools pull the maker into detail too early.
principles.apply: State the limit in the round header and keep final copy, color and imagery out of the round.
principles.test: Each exploration round states its limit and contains no final copy, color or imagery.

principles.title: Answer vagueness with a sketch
principles.rule: When a request is abstract, answer with one or two quick concrete interpretations and ask which is closer before investing in a design.
principles.why: People who cannot describe an idea will still correct a wrong drawing.
principles.apply: Make the guesses deliberately rough and different so the correction is informative.
principles.test: Abstract requests receive a concrete rough guess and a confirm question before full work.

principles.title: Mark drafts as drafts
principles.rule: Show concept work in a visibly unfinished form with a draft label when you want feedback on the idea.
principles.why: Rough work invites comment on the concept; pixel-perfect work signals that decisions are closed.
principles.apply: Pair each concept review request with the words concept, not style.
principles.test: Concept-review artifacts carry a draft label and no final styling.

principles.title: Review early, mid and late
principles.rule: Schedule at least three reviews per project, with the first one before any high-fidelity work.
principles.why: Early review stops long investment in a wrong idea.
principles.apply: Put the three review points in the plan at kickoff.
principles.test: The plan shows three or more review points and the first predates high-fidelity work.

principles.title: Never stage a big reveal
principles.rule: Let no more than one fidelity step pass between user checkpoints, so the first view of the design is never the final deliverable.
principles.why: By the time work is polished, the maker is too invested to listen and reviewers can only approve or reject.
principles.apply: Show the box or outline stage before the styled stage, and the styled stage before the coded one.
principles.test: No fidelity level is skipped between two user checkpoints.

principles.title: Frame then ask specific questions
principles.rule: Open every review with the user goal, the business goal and the constraints, then ask the specific questions you need answered.
principles.why: Reviewers who lack the goals give unusable feedback, and open requests turn critique into brainstorming.
principles.apply: Default: one to four questions per review.
principles.test: Each review request begins with the three framing items and lists explicit questions.

principles.title: Frame, then stop pitching
principles.rule: Show the work after the framing without persuasion or a walkthrough of how to read it, and record feedback before rebutting any of it.
principles.why: Explanation spends the reviewer's fresh eye.
principles.apply: In the chat, put the artifact and the questions first, and answer objections only in the next turn.
principles.test: The text before the artifact holds only framing and questions, and no feedback is rebutted in the turn it arrives.

principles.title: Critique ties element to goal
principles.rule: Write each critique item as an element, an observation and the goal it helps or harms, never a bare like or dislike.
principles.why: A tied observation tells the maker what to weigh.
principles.apply: Rewrite any taste-only comment into the element, observation and goal form before logging it.
principles.test: Every logged critique item names an element, an observation and an affected goal.

principles.title: Critique the work, not maker
principles.rule: Make the design the subject of every critique sentence, never the person who made it.
principles.why: Wording aimed at the maker breeds defensiveness and stops sharing.
principles.apply: Write findings as the layout does or the header lacks, not you did.
principles.test: No critique sentence has the maker as its subject.

principles.title: Problems before solutions
principles.rule: List what works and what needs refinement first, and offer fixes only in a separate optional block.
principles.why: Solutions from reviewers move the decision away from the maker and invite design by committee.
principles.apply: In the review file, keep a working-well list, a needs-refinement list and an optional suggestions block.
principles.test: Each critique has non-empty working-well and needs-refinement lists, with fixes kept separate.

principles.title: Separate maker and critic
principles.rule: Keep the role that made the work apart from the role that critiques it, and log all feedback for the maker afterwards.
principles.why: The maker is biased toward its own work and needs to listen.
principles.apply: When subagents exist, run the critique in a separate critic context; otherwise reread the brief fresh and label the review single-context.
principles.test: The review record names maker and critic as different roles, or is labelled single-context.

principles.title: Retrospect into harness changes
principles.rule: After each project, record what worked, what did not and what to change, and turn each change into a proposed edit to a skill, rule or catalog.
principles.why: Lessons are lost unless they are written down and acted on.
principles.apply: Ask the user the three questions first, add your own answers, then file the proposals for approval.
principles.test: A closed project has a retrospective with three lists and at least one proposed harness change or a reason for none.

principles.title: Prototype only open questions
principles.rule: Scope each prototype to the parts you have the most questions about and stub the rest.
principles.why: A full-product prototype spends time on parts that test nothing.
principles.apply: List the open questions at the top of the prototype and check each screen against them.
principles.test: Every screen or flow in the prototype serves a listed open question.

principles.title: Rough for peers, real for users
principles.rule: Keep concept prototypes rough for colleagues, but make prototypes for end-user tests realistic enough that the tester forgets it is a prototype.
principles.why: End users react to roughness instead of the experience.
principles.apply: For a user test, use realistic content and data and run it on the target device.
principles.test: An end-user test prototype has realistic content, runs on the target device and contains no filler.

principles.title: Cheap enough to throw away
principles.rule: Keep each prototype cheap enough that you will still change or discard it when feedback demands.
principles.why: A costly prototype makes the maker resist the feedback it was built to get.
principles.apply: Use free or owned tools first and wait for a tested direction before any paid generation.
principles.test: The prototype's build cost is recorded and no paid generation precedes a tested direction.

principles.title: Check feasibility before users
principles.rule: Get a builder's feasibility check, covering data availability, required fields and platform limits, before putting a prototype in front of users.
principles.why: Testing an unbuildable design wastes the testers and the team.
principles.apply: Hand the prototype to the coding agent or code owner for a short feasibility note.
principles.test: A feasibility note exists and predates the first user test.

principles.title: Show it on the target device
principles.rule: Review and test the prototype on the device class and viewport it is meant for, not only on a desktop canvas.
principles.why: The real device gives the real experience.
principles.apply: Capture the render at the target viewport for every review of a device-specific design.
principles.test: Review captures come from the target viewport or device class.

principles.title: Small rounds, repeated
principles.rule: Test with a small group of users per round, revise, and test again rather than running one large round.
principles.why: A handful of users exposes most problems, and several small rounds beat one big one.
principles.apply: Default: about five users per round, with a logged revision between rounds.
principles.test: Each test round has a small participant count and a logged revision before the next round.

principles.title: Script tests, never help
principles.rule: Run user tests from a written script with welcome, warm-up, introduction, tasks and debrief, and give no hints during tasks.
principles.why: A helpful moderator contaminates the result.
principles.apply: Write the script before recruiting and keep a moderator log.
principles.test: A five-part script exists and the session notes show no hints during tasks.

principles.title: Confirm data fields exist
principles.rule: Before high-fidelity design of any data-driven view or form, confirm that every displayed field exists and is available, and get the required field list from the code or its owner.
principles.why: A polished dashboard is gutted when the data it shows does not exist.
principles.apply: Make a field list for each data view and check it against the API or schema with the coding agent.
principles.test: Every field shown in the design appears in a confirmed field list.

principles.title: Flows follow user tasks
principles.rule: Name navigation and flows after user tasks from the job stories, not after tables, endpoints or data models.
principles.why: Designing over the database yields good-looking screens with confusing flows.
principles.apply: Review the flow names against the job stories before any styling.
principles.test: Navigation and flow names match user tasks, and none is a table or endpoint name.

principles.title: Write named design values
principles.rule: Write a short named list of design values for the project and cite one by name whenever a contested choice is defended.
principles.why: Shared values let a detail be justified in terms everyone accepted.
principles.apply: Default: four to six values. Remove a choice that serves no value and no goal.
principles.test: Each contested decision in the record cites a named design value.

principles.title: Pair maker with critic
principles.rule: Run substantial design work as a pair: a lead maker and a partner who critiques and unsticks.
principles.why: Pairs explore more and recover faster than lone makers.
principles.apply: With subagents, run a maker and a critic agent with one named as lead.
principles.test: Each substantial task names a lead and a partner or critic.

principles.title: Keep work visibly in progress
principles.rule: Keep work in progress in a shared place the user can open at any time, with versions and notes, not only the latest polished state.
principles.why: Hidden work becomes a black box that stakeholders misread or ignore.
principles.apply: Save each round to the project folder with its notes and rejected options.
principles.test: The project folder holds every round in order with notes and rejected options.

principles.title: Seek feedback, keep the decision
principles.rule: Collect feedback from anyone, then give each item a decision of accepted, rejected or deferred with a reason tied to a goal, value or evidence.
principles.why: Good ideas come from anywhere, but committee design comes from changing things only because someone asked.
principles.apply: Hold final authority with the user and still state the trade-off before applying a change that harms the goals.
principles.test: Every feedback item has a recorded decision and reason, and no change cites only that someone asked.

principles.title: Argue in the listener's terms
principles.rule: Justify each recommendation to a non-designer by the goal it serves for them, never by taste words alone.
principles.why: Executives and makers judge by different criteria, and taste words persuade only designers.
principles.apply: Replace words such as cleaner or more modern with the user goal or business goal the choice serves.
principles.test: Each recommendation to a non-designer names the stated goal it serves.

principles.title: Listen before directing
principles.rule: Ask about goals, audience and constraints and restate the answers before proposing any direction.
principles.why: A direction offered before listening answers the wrong question.
principles.apply: In the first turn, propose a direction only if the user already supplied all three.
principles.test: The first proposal of an engagement follows a restatement of goals, audience and constraints.

principles.title: Delegate priorities, not steps
principles.rule: Give a sub-agent or tool the goal, the ordered priorities, the principles and the hard constraints, and leave the execution open.
principles.why: People and agents do better work when they own how it gets done.
principles.apply: Write delegation prompts as an ordered priority list plus constraints, with no step list unless a step is a hard constraint.
principles.test: Each delegation brief has a goal, ordered priorities and constraints, and lists steps only for hard constraints.

principles.title: Commit and state the doubt
principles.rule: Make one clear recommendation and name the one condition that would change it.
principles.why: A list of options without a choice shifts the work back to the user, and false certainty hides risk.
principles.apply: End each option set with a labelled recommendation and its changing condition.
principles.test: Each recommendation names one choice and one condition that would reverse it.

principles.title: Three questions before changing inherited work
principles.rule: Before changing an existing brand, system or product, ask what works, what does not work and what to focus on, and keep what the user says works.
principles.why: Changing inherited work at once destroys what was right about it.
principles.apply: Ask each owner of part of the work separately and record the answers before the first proposal.
principles.test: For inherited work, the log holds the three answers dated before the first proposed change.

principles.title: Label every constraint's source
principles.rule: List the technical, brand, legal, time, budget and platform constraints and mark each as stated by the user, found in the project or assumed.
principles.why: Work cannot fit a limit nobody named, and an assumed limit can shrink the space for no reason.
principles.apply: Challenge each assumed constraint once before designing around it.
principles.test: The brief's constraint list tags every entry with its source.

principles.title: Seed principles with examples
principles.rule: Open a principles discussion with candidate principles drawn from comparable work and your own drafts, not with a blank question.
principles.why: A seed gives people something to react to and shows how a principle changes the work.
principles.apply: Offer candidates, let the user write theirs, then group, vote and describe each kept one in a sentence.
principles.test: The principles thread starts with seeded candidates and ends with a short list where each item has a description.

principles.title: Rank yours before seeing theirs
principles.rule: Record each person's input separately, and write your own ranking down before you read the user's.
principles.why: Groups conform to the loudest voice, and an agent anchors on what it reads first.
principles.apply: When several people give input, log each with a name before any group discussion.
principles.test: Each participant's input and the agent's ranking are recorded before the discussion that uses them.

principles.title: Check values against the work
principles.rule: At each milestone, point to where each project principle shows in the current work and flag principles with no evidence.
principles.why: Principles that describe a wish rather than the work stop guiding it.
principles.apply: Ask the user to drop or reword any principle that has no visible evidence.
principles.test: Each principle in the project file maps to a place in the current work or is flagged.

principles.title: Bring in outside perspectives
principles.rule: Include at least one reviewer or reference from outside the project's category or discipline.
principles.why: Sameness in the inputs produces sameness in the output.
principles.apply: Add an out-of-category reference to every board and an outside role to major reviews.
principles.test: The reference set and reviewer list each include one source from outside the category.

principles.title: Write a not-this-round list
principles.rule: Keep an explicit list of what is out of scope for this round, and finish each item in scope to the agreed bar before starting a new one.
principles.why: Doing fewer things protects quality.
principles.apply: Move scope creep from feedback into the list instead of acting on it.
principles.test: The scope section has a not-in-this-round list and no item in it was worked on.

principles.title: Log build-driven simplifications
principles.rule: Record every simplification made for ease of build with what the user loses, and get the user's acceptance.
principles.why: Under build pressure, designs drift silently toward the easiest path.
principles.apply: Add a simplifications list to the handoff and review it with the user.
principles.test: Each simplification for build reasons appears with its cost and an acceptance.

principles.title: One system across surfaces
principles.rule: Review work that spans products or platforms in one pass against the same token and component set.
principles.why: Surfaces designed apart drift apart.
principles.apply: Lay every surface side by side in one review and list deviations from the shared system.
principles.test: A multi-surface deliverable has one review that compares every surface with the same system.

principles.title: Name the mode: explore or refine
principles.rule: State whether a task is exploration or refinement, and keep refinement changes inside scope while exploration produces more than one concept.
principles.why: An explorer asked to polish redesigns everything, and a polisher asked to explore produces one safe option.
principles.apply: Put the mode in the brief and park out-of-scope ideas from refine rounds in a separate list.
principles.test: The brief states the mode; refine rounds touch only in-scope elements and explore rounds show several concepts.

principles.title: Bound open exploration
principles.rule: Give open exploration a time box, a concept count, at least one fixed constraint and a check-in before the box ends.
principles.why: Unbounded freedom stalls and stresses the work.
principles.apply: Pick the fixed constraint from the brief, such as the medium or the subject.
principles.test: Each exploration task states a time box, a count, a fixed constraint and a check-in.

principles.title: Probe a quiet approval
principles.rule: When a reply to a review is short or neutral, ask one specific question about a named part of the work before treating it as approval.
principles.why: Silence often hides an unvoiced issue.
principles.apply: Name the part you are least sure of and ask about it directly.
principles.test: Every short or neutral reply is followed by one specific question before the work moves on.

principles.title: Confirm relayed feedback
principles.rule: Mark feedback passed on from a third party as relayed, and get the original wording or a direct confirmation before a major change.
principles.why: Second-hand reports grow in the retelling.
principles.apply: Ask the user for the exact words or for the person to comment directly.
principles.test: Relayed feedback is tagged and major changes cite a confirmation.

principles.title: Settle conflicts side by side
principles.rule: When two inputs conflict, list them side by side with their sources and ask the user for a decision before the next milestone.
principles.why: Unresolved conflict reappears later as rework.
principles.apply: Record the decision in design/decisions.md with both inputs.
principles.test: No conflict between inputs stays open past the next milestone.

principles.title: Label each artifact's status
principles.rule: Label every shared artifact with its status, such as exploration, direction or final candidate, and ask polish questions only of high-fidelity work.
principles.why: Pixel-perfect comps read as finished and hold back structural feedback.
principles.apply: Choose the fidelity to show from the feedback you want, then label it.
principles.test: Every shared artifact carries a status label that matches the questions asked.

principles.title: Review motion in its medium
principles.rule: Review interaction, animation and responsive behavior in a running or recorded version at more than one viewport, not in a still image.
principles.why: These qualities do not survive a static image.
principles.apply: For code deliverables, capture at each breakpoint; for an artifact type, follow that type's own check rule.
principles.test: Each review of motion, interaction or responsive work used a running version at two or more viewports.

principles.title: Impartial failure review
principles.rule: Have someone other than the maker facilitate the review of a failed project, built on a shared timeline and blaming no person.
principles.why: A maker grading its own failure misses the cause.
principles.apply: Use a separate reviewer agent or the user as facilitator, and give each lesson an owner and a date.
principles.test: The failure review names a facilitator who did not do the work, and each action has an owner and a date.

principles.title: Collect adjacent-role context
principles.rule: Before designing, gather what research, sales, product and support each know about customers, schedule and pain points.
principles.why: Each adjacent role holds knowledge design needs and rarely volunteers.
principles.apply: Add one brief line per role with the finding or not available.
principles.test: The brief has one line each for research, sales, product and support.

principles.title: Show how the design was reached
principles.rule: Include a short plain-language account of the problem, the options considered and the reason for the choice in every presentation.
principles.why: People who see the path can take part in the decision.
principles.apply: Write the account without undefined design terms.
principles.test: Each presentation includes problem, options and reason in plain language.

principles.title: Vision answers why, through a person
principles.rule: Write the vision as a short story of one specific person using the product in their own setting, answering why it should exist, with no feature list or schedule.
principles.why: Teams sprinting through iterations lose sight of the life the product fits into.
principles.apply: Ground it in at least one observed behavior, or label it hypothesis.
principles.test: The vision names a person, a setting and a moment of use, cites an observation or says hypothesis, and lists no features.

principles.title: Cheapest medium that guides
principles.rule: Make the vision in the cheapest medium with enough fidelity to guide the work, such as a style board, storyboard or short motion piece.
principles.why: The story matters more than the medium, and an expensive vision delays the work it should guide.
principles.apply: Keep vision production small next to the project length and state the medium and why.
principles.test: The vision artifact states its medium and reason, and its effort is small next to the project.

principles.title: Fix the destination, free the route
principles.rule: State the intended experience in the vision and leave screens, components and implementation to the people who build them.
principles.why: A destination aligns teams while each keeps room to solve its own part.
principles.apply: Strike layouts and component choices from the vision artifact.
principles.test: The vision contains no screen layouts or implementation detail.

principles.title: Test decisions against the vision
principles.rule: Check each major decision against the vision and flag any decision that does not serve it.
principles.why: Without a fixed reference, the work accumulates mess.
principles.apply: Add a serves-the-vision line to each major entry in design/decisions.md.
principles.test: Each major decision in the record says how it serves the vision or is flagged.

principles.title: Think by making
principles.rule: Present every direction with at least one visual artifact, such as a sketch, board, storyboard or prototype, never prose alone.
principles.why: Making informs thinking, and a vision seen is stronger than one described.
principles.apply: Pair each direction's description with a rough visual, even a box sketch.
principles.test: Every presented direction includes at least one visual artifact.

principles.title: Let work be torn down
principles.rule: Before refining, let a direction be broken apart and rebuilt at least once, and do not polish the first assembly.
principles.why: Deconstructing and rebuilding a whole idea is a core source of design value that delivery pressure suppresses.
principles.apply: In explore rounds, take the strongest direction, remove its central device and rebuild it another way as a sibling option.
principles.test: The record shows a rebuilt variant of a direction before that direction was refined.

principles.title: Options side by side
principles.rule: Show options together in one view, such as a board, contact sheet or comparison page, never one at a time.
principles.why: Ideas collide and compare only when they sit together.
principles.apply: Build each option round as one comparison artifact with equal framing for every option.
principles.test: Each option round is presented in a single side-by-side view.

principles.title: Judge by need, not schedule
principles.rule: Mark the delivery checklist pass or fail on at least one criterion tied to the stated user need, not only on whether it shipped on time.
principles.why: Teams measured only on delivery ship subpar products on schedule.
principles.apply: Copy the user need from the brief into the finalize checklist with its evidence.
principles.test: The delivery checklist has a user-need criterion marked pass or fail with evidence.

principles.title: Choose tools for craft first
principles.rule: Pick a tool for what it does well for the design task, and treat already connected only as a tiebreaker.
principles.why: Tools chosen for integration convenience degrade the craft.
principles.apply: Write the design task each candidate tool does best before routing work to it.
principles.test: Each tool choice in the plan names the design task it does well.

principles.title: Scope every review up front
principles.rule: Open every review artifact with four lines: the feedback wanted, from whom, what feedback is not useful now, and what is locked.
principles.why: Stating scope first prevents late, off-stage and out-of-scope comments.
principles.apply: Write the block before showing any work and sort incoming comments into in scope, parked or against a locked item.
principles.test: Every review artifact begins with the four-line scope block.

principles.title: Grow a locked list
principles.rule: Declare which elements are final at each gate, and answer a change request against a locked item with an explicit reopen question and its cost.
principles.why: Reopening settled decisions silently burns the schedule and the team.
principles.apply: Keep the locked list in design/decisions.md and extend it after each round.
principles.test: The locked list grows at each gate, and every change to a locked item follows a recorded reopen decision.

principles.title: One decider per aspect
principles.rule: Name one final decision maker for each aspect of the output, such as brand, copy and technical, and hear everyone else as input.
principles.why: Two deciders for one aspect means no decision.
principles.apply: Put the decider table in the brief at kickoff.
principles.test: The brief names exactly one decider for each aspect.

principles.title: Feedback type follows stage
principles.rule: Tell reviewers which kind of feedback fits each stage, such as direction at concept and detail at refinement.
principles.why: Detail notes at concept stage and direction notes at the end both waste a round.
principles.apply: List allowed feedback types per stage in the plan and repeat them in each review request.
principles.test: Each stage in the plan lists its allowed feedback types.

principles.title: Force a strict ranking
principles.rule: Rank deliverables in strict order with no ties at the top, and refuse an everything-is-urgent list.
principles.why: When every request is high priority, the work spreads thin.
principles.apply: Ask the user to order the list; propose an order when they will not.
principles.test: A multi-deliverable plan carries a strict order with no shared first place.

principles.title: Light path for small work
principles.rule: Scale process to the job: run a light path for a single small asset and the full path for a brand or product, and record which one and why.
principles.why: Heavy process on small fast work costs more than it saves.
principles.apply: Decide the path at intake from the scope and the number of deliverables.
principles.test: The project record states light or full path with a reason.

principles.title: Restate and challenge the request
principles.rule: At intake, restate the problem in your own words and raise at least one challenge or question about the request itself.
principles.why: Makers who only execute become operators of other people's solutions.
principles.apply: Put the restatement and the challenge in the brief before planning.
principles.test: The intake output holds a restatement and at least one challenge to the request.

principles.title: Spare the maker bookkeeping
principles.rule: Do the filing, naming, status and license tracking yourself and never ask the user to do bookkeeping the harness can do.
principles.why: Operations exists to protect the maker's time and attention.
principles.apply: Keep the asset manifest, status file and decision log up to date without prompting.
principles.test: The session contains no request that the user file, name or track something the harness could.

principles.title: Design QA before launch
principles.rule: Run a dated design QA against the spec and the design system before any launch, and record the approver and the version approved.
principles.why: A launch with no QA record ships its defects unseen.
principles.apply: Make QA the last step of finalize and archive the project after approval.
principles.test: Each launch has a dated QA result and an approval naming approver and version.

principles.title: Visual status, not prose
principles.rule: Send status updates that show the current artifact for each active item, plus progress, blockers and the decisions needed.
principles.why: People track work by seeing it, and a decision request buried in prose waits.
principles.apply: Keep the update to one screen with an image or link per item.
principles.test: Each status update holds a visual per active item and a decisions-needed line.

principles.title: End critique with owned actions
principles.rule: Close every critique with a numbered action list in which each action has an owner.
principles.why: A critique without next steps changes nothing.
principles.apply: Copy the actions into the next round's plan and tick them off there.
principles.test: Each critique log ends with numbered, owned actions.

principles.title: Enforce a naming convention
principles.rule: Fix a file naming convention and folder structure for the project and check every file against it.
principles.why: Names and folders decide whether anything can be found later.
principles.apply: Create the project folders from the standard structure at kickoff and lint names before handoff.
principles.test: A naming check over the project files reports zero violations.

principles.title: Record every decision path
principles.rule: Log each direction change with the options considered, the choice and the reason.
principles.why: Documentation, decision paths and archives are what make design work repeatable.
principles.apply: Write the entry in design/decisions.md in the same turn as the change.
principles.test: Every direction change in the record lists options, choice and reason.

principles.title: Drop check-ins that change nothing
principles.rule: Review each recurring check-in or ritual and remove the ones that never changed a decision.
principles.why: Unneeded rituals tax the people doing the work.
principles.apply: Ask this in every retrospective and update the project rhythm.
principles.test: The retrospective records whether each recurring check-in changed a decision.

principles.title: Search past research first
principles.rule: Search the project's research and prior work for the question before running any new research, and log the search.
principles.why: A repository stops the team asking the same question twice.
principles.apply: Give each research note metadata for project, date, source, method and topic.
principles.test: Each new research call is preceded by a logged search of existing material.

principles.title: Insights apart from data
principles.rule: Write insights as their own file, each linked to the observations that support it.
principles.why: Insights, not raw data, are research's most valuable output.
principles.apply: Keep raw notes and the insight list separate and link every insight back.
principles.test: An insights file exists and every insight links to its supporting items.

principles.title: Track licenses, spend and fallbacks
principles.rule: Keep each tool's license terms, cost model, approval rule and fallback in the catalog, and get the user's approval before any spend.
principles.why: Untracked tools create surprise charges, lost access and dead ends.
principles.apply: Let the user set a spend ceiling for routine calls and log every spend against it.
principles.test: No spend in the project log lacks an approval or a ceiling that covers it.

principles.title: Consent for real people
principles.rule: Record consent or a license for every asset that shows a real person's face, voice or likeness before it is used.
principles.why: Releases are legal requirements, not courtesy.
principles.apply: Add a consent field to each asset in design/assets/manifest.json.
principles.test: Every asset showing a real person has a consent or license note in the manifest.

principles.title: Say flare or focus
principles.rule: State in every phase whether the work is widening the options or narrowing them, and do not narrow while you claim to be widening.
principles.why: Design alternates between flaring and focusing, and mixing the two kills ideas early.
principles.apply: Head each round with flare or focus and match the output count to it.
principles.test: Every round header says flare or focus, and flare rounds add options rather than cut them.

principles.title: Start where the project stands
principles.rule: When a draft or product already exists, start by testing it as a prototype instead of restarting from research.

principles.apply: Ask at intake what exists and pick the entry phase from the answer.
principles.test: The plan names its entry phase and the reason for it.

principles.title: Build sure, test doubtful
principles.rule: Make each prototype as if you are right, then test it as if you are wrong.
principles.why: Conviction gives the build energy, and doubt makes the test honest.
principles.apply: Write down before testing what result would prove the direction wrong.
principles.test: Each test plan states the result that would disprove the direction.

source.part: Chapter 1: Why we need design thinking

principles.title: First idea is a hypothesis
principles.rule: Record the first solution idea, the user's or yours, as a hypothesis with at least one observation that would disprove it.
principles.why: First concepts are often wrong in ways only evidence shows.
principles.apply: Put the hypothesis and its disproof in the brief and look for the disproof first.
principles.test: The brief lists the initial idea with a disconfirming observation to look for.

principles.title: Get close to real use
principles.rule: Collect at least one source from the real setting of use, such as a screen recording, photos of the place, or a walk-through.
principles.why: Context exposes constraints that an interview alone hides, such as hurry, noise or a weak connection.
principles.apply: Ask the user for a recording or photos before deciding layout and density.
principles.test: The research notes include at least one source captured in the real context.

principles.title: Hunt workarounds and extreme users
principles.rule: Ask who uses the product far more, far less or in an odd way, and what workarounds people invent, before defining the need.
principles.why: Extreme behavior shows a need in its strongest form and often points to the core idea.
principles.apply: Turn each workaround into a candidate insight in the synthesis.
principles.test: The notes list at least one workaround or extreme-user behavior, or record that none was found.

principles.title: Record fears and delights
principles.rule: Describe the people served with at least one fear and one moment of delight tied to the situation, not only their tasks.
principles.why: Feelings decide adoption and can block the task entirely.
principles.apply: Carry the named fear and delight into the brief's emotion targets.
principles.test: The user description names at least one fear and one delight.

principles.title: Shrink research, never skip
principles.rule: When time is short, run the single cheapest empathy activity that fits, such as one interview or one walk-through, instead of skipping research.
principles.why: Even quick observation can change the outcome.
principles.apply: Write three findings and one surprise from it and feed them to the definition.
principles.test: A constrained project still shows one empathy activity and its findings.

principles.title: Patterns before problem statements
principles.rule: Group raw observations into named patterns and write one insight per pattern before defining the problem.
principles.why: Insights come from patterns across observations, not from single remarks.
principles.apply: Keep the link from each insight to its observations.
principles.test: A synthesis note groups observations under named patterns with linked insights.

principles.title: State the need without the product
principles.rule: Write the need so it still makes sense after every product, channel and format word is removed.
principles.why: Naming the format in the need caps the solution space.
principles.apply: If the need says website, app or video, rewrite it as the change the person needs.
principles.test: Removing every product noun from the need statement leaves a sentence that still makes sense.

principles.title: Name the target feeling
principles.rule: End the point of view with how the person should feel when the need is met.
principles.why: The feeling clause steers tone, visuals and features.
principles.apply: Pick one precise word, such as relieved, proud or in control, and one feeling to avoid.
principles.test: The point of view or brief contains a clause naming the target feeling.

principles.title: Reframe before you ideate
principles.rule: Write at least two framings of the problem, including one zoomed out to a wider goal and one zoomed in to the sharpest moment, and compare the directions each opens.
principles.why: Reframing is the main route to answers that are not obvious.
principles.apply: Show the framings side by side with the solution directions each allows, and record why one was chosen.
principles.test: The record shows two or more framings and a reason for the chosen one.

principles.title: Name who it is not for
principles.rule: State in the brief who the work is not for and whose need loses when two groups want opposite things.
principles.why: Designing for everyone is impossible and produces the average answer.
principles.apply: Use the exclusion to break ties between directions.
principles.test: The brief names at least one group the work is not for.

principles.title: Map before and after
principles.rule: Map the experience from before the person meets the design to after they leave it, and mark which touchpoints the project can change.
principles.why: The experience is wider than the artifact, and the earliest moments often carry the most fear.
principles.apply: Target the touchpoints with the highest emotional stakes.
principles.test: A journey list covers before, during and after with each touchpoint marked changeable or fixed.

principles.title: POV must pick a winner
principles.rule: Test the point of view by applying it to two competing ideas, and sharpen it until it favors one of them.
principles.why: A statement that fits every idea guides no decision.
principles.apply: Rewrite the point of view when both ideas pass it equally.
principles.test: Applied to two sample ideas, the point of view favors one with a stated reason.

principles.title: Questions from the POV
principles.rule: Derive several how-might-we questions from phrases of the point of view, each narrower than the whole problem and none naming a solution.
principles.why: Good questions give each ideation round a clear target.
principles.apply: Rank them with the user and take the top one as the first round's mission.
principles.test: Each question traces to a phrase of the point of view and names no solution.

principles.title: Generate first, judge later
principles.rule: Keep evaluation and feasibility comments out of the generation phase entirely.
principles.why: Early judgment suppresses the odd ideas that become the good ones.
principles.apply: Write all options, then switch to a separate selection step.
principles.test: No evaluation or feasibility remark appears in the generation phase of the round.

principles.title: Quantity target and time box
principles.rule: Give each ideation topic a time box and a numeric idea target, and report the actual count.
principles.why: Limits keep energy up and quantity raises the odds of a good idea.
principles.apply: Default: about 15 to 20 minutes or an equal effort budget per topic.
principles.test: Each round states its time box and target and reports the count reached.

principles.title: Headline every idea
principles.rule: Give each idea a few-word headline and a thumbnail or one-line visual description, and share one idea at a time.
principles.why: Headlines and sketches make ideas easy to capture, compare and group.
principles.apply: Number the ideas and park off-topic ones in a visible list.
principles.test: Every idea in the round has a headline and a visual description.

principles.title: Select across several criteria
principles.rule: Pick ideas under several named criteria, such as easiest win, most delightful and long shot, without cutting for feasibility first.
principles.why: Ideas that look silly can seed good ones, and one criterion selects only the safe.
principles.apply: Make your picks next to the user's and require a different idea for each label.
principles.test: The selection shows a pick per criterion and no idea was cut for feasibility beforehand.

principles.title: Never carry only the safest
principles.rule: Take two or more ideas into prototyping, and make sure at least one is not the lowest-risk choice.
principles.why: Prototyping flares again, and a single safe build has nothing to be compared with.
principles.apply: Label the risk level of each idea taken forward.
principles.test: Two or more ideas enter prototyping and at least one is not the lowest-risk option.

principles.title: Keep the wild idea's appeal
principles.rule: For each wild idea you reject, write what is attractive in it and look for a buildable way to keep that quality.
principles.why: The appeal often survives even when the literal idea cannot be built.
principles.apply: Fold the named quality into one of the directions taken forward.
principles.test: Each rejected wild idea has a one-line note on its attractive quality.

principles.title: Question and decision rule first
principles.rule: Before building a prototype, write the question it answers and the result that would change the plan.
principles.why: A prototype is good only if it helps answer a question.
principles.apply: Reduce the question to its simplest example and build that with tools you already know.
principles.test: Every prototype has a written question and a plan-changing result.

principles.title: Time-box two or three variants
principles.rule: Build two or three low-resolution variations inside a short time box before investing in one.
principles.why: A time box forces focus, and variants give a comparison.
principles.apply: Default: about an hour of effort for the first variants.
principles.test: The round states its time box and produced two or three variations.

principles.title: Fake the hard part by hand
principles.rule: Simulate the costly part of a product, such as an algorithm or a service, by hand behind the interface while you still learn what people need.
principles.why: A hand-run back end teaches how people ask for things before anything is built.
principles.apply: List what is simulated in the prototype brief and log how users phrase their requests.
principles.test: The prototype brief lists every hand-simulated part.

principles.title: Polish can be function
principles.rule: Do not mark feedback cues, transitions or other polish optional until you have tested what they do.
principles.why: An animated transition can fix a real defect, such as a delay with no feedback on a slow network.
principles.apply: Give every state with a delay or change a feedback cue and test it under poor conditions.
principles.test: Every delayed or changing state in the prototype has a tested feedback cue.

principles.title: Test symbols per locale
principles.rule: Test icons, labels and key terms with each target audience and locale before build.
principles.why: A familiar icon can read as something else in another market.
principles.apply: List each locale with the icons and terms checked there in the test plan.
principles.test: The test plan lists each locale or audience with its checked icons and terms.

principles.title: Demonstrate, don't chart
principles.rule: To make one point clear, build the simplest demonstration that shows it and strip anything that carries no data.
principles.why: A plain demonstration lands where a cluttered chart fails.
principles.apply: Ask whether the audience can restate the point after seeing it.
principles.test: Each key message has one plain demonstration or view with no decoration that carries no data.

principles.title: Show before you explain
principles.rule: Present the artifact and a task first, and explain intent only after the reaction.
principles.why: You need a reaction to the experience, not to your explanation.
principles.apply: Open the review message with the work and one task, and hold the rationale for later.
principles.test: The first message of a review presents the artifact and a task with no rationale.

principles.title: Bring two to every test
principles.rule: Show at least two options in a test and record the comparison.
principles.why: People compare more easily than they judge one thing alone.
principles.apply: Ask for the gut reaction before any considered opinion.
principles.test: Each test shows two or more options and records the comparison.

principles.title: Tag every claim's evidence
principles.rule: Tag each claim about users in the brief as observed, reported or assumed.
principles.why: Admitting what you do not know is the start of finding out.
principles.apply: Treat the user's account of their customers as reported, not observed, and plan one outside check.
principles.test: Every claim about users in the brief carries an evidence tag.

principles.title: Review harm and misuse
principles.rule: Write a short review of how the design could harm, shame or be misused by the people who use it.
principles.why: Designers share responsibility for the consequences of use.
principles.apply: Update the review after each test round.
principles.test: The brief contains a harm and misuse review.

principles.title: Climb the four needs in order
principles.rule: Check every core task for function, reliability and usability before adding pleasure, and block pleasure work on any task that fails the first three.
principles.why: A person who cannot finish a task never stays to feel anything good.
principles.apply: Record pass or fail for each layer per task in the review.
principles.test: Each core task has a pass for function, reliability and usability before any pleasure element is added to it.

principles.title: Go past usable on purpose
principles.rule: Give every deliverable at least one deliberate element whose job is emotional, and name the feeling it targets.
principles.why: Usable is the floor; pleasure is what people remember and recommend.
principles.apply: Pick the element from copy, illustration, motion or interaction and record it in the design notes.
principles.test: The design notes name at least one emotional element per deliverable and its target feeling.

principles.title: Cut delight that blocks tasks
principles.rule: Remove or move any emotional element that adds a step, covers a control, delays feedback or hides a status.
principles.why: Delight that harms function turns a good moment into a complaint.
principles.apply: Count steps and time with and without the element.
principles.test: No emotional element adds a step, hides a control or delays feedback.

principles.title: Find the ownable moments
principles.rule: List the steps where the user's emotion changes sharply, up or down, with the expected emotion and the planned response for each.
principles.why: A small, well-placed response at those points has an outsized effect for little cost.
principles.apply: Design these moments first; they are where the product's character shows.
principles.test: A list of ownable moments exists with step, emotion, direction and response for each.

principles.title: Meet the emotion of the moment
principles.rule: Change copy and behavior at each ownable moment to match the user's state, such as a plain condolence at a loss or a real celebration after a long task.
principles.why: People forgive, follow and recommend a product that recognizes how they feel.
principles.apply: Write the moment's copy from the user's state, not from the default component text.
principles.test: At each ownable moment the text or behavior differs from the default pattern and fits the expected emotion.

principles.title: Pleasure only where needs meet
principles.rule: Tie every reward, streak or notification to a benefit for the user, and remove any whose only beneficiary is the business.
principles.why: The same loop that builds a helpful habit powers manipulative mechanics.
principles.apply: Write the user benefit in one sentence next to each engagement mechanic.
principles.test: Each reward, streak and notification has a written user benefit.

principles.title: Do not ship framework defaults
principles.rule: Never call a look finished while its type, color, spacing and components are all the unmodified defaults of the framework or library used.
principles.why: Defaults make products impossible to tell apart.
principles.apply: Compare the output with the library's stock theme and change the choices the design system does not fix.
principles.test: At least one of type, color, spacing or component styling differs from the library default, or the design system prescribes the default.

principles.title: Contrast marks what matters
principles.rule: Use strong contrast only on the few elements that matter most, and give every high-contrast element a stated priority.
principles.why: The eye scans for breaks in pattern to decide what matters.
principles.apply: Run a squint or five-second look at the render and compare what is seen first with the priority list.
principles.test: The first elements a viewer names match the intended priority order.

principles.title: One loud element per view
principles.rule: Let only one element per view carry the primary visual weight, and demote any rival that competes with it.
principles.why: When everything shouts, nothing is heard.
principles.apply: Name the single primary action of each view in the design notes.
principles.test: A reviewer can name the single primary action of each view.

principles.title: Remove choices before adding
principles.rule: Count navigation items, calls to action and promotional blocks per view, and justify any increase with a user task.
principles.why: Decision time grows with the number of options.
principles.apply: Default: four choices per decision point as the kit target.
principles.test: Any increase in choices per view carries a written reason tied to a user task.

principles.title: Simulate color vision deficiency
principles.rule: Run status and category colors through a color vision deficiency simulation and keep every pair distinguishable.
principles.why: Contrast some users cannot see fails as contrast.
principles.apply: Add a second cue such as an icon, label or position for status colors.
principles.test: Status and category pairs stay distinguishable in a color vision deficiency simulation.

principles.title: Notify only for user action
principles.rule: Send a notification, badge or alert only when the user needs to act on it, and keep promotional interruptions off by default.
principles.why: Notifications borrow the instinct for contrast; misused, they bury the ones that matter.
principles.apply: List each notification type with its user-side trigger and action.
principles.test: Every notification type has a user-side trigger and action, and none is promotional by default.

principles.title: Aesthetics is part of usability
principles.rule: Run a separate aesthetic pass with named criteria such as proportion, type, color, spacing and finish, and never defer it as decoration.
principles.why: Attractive things put people in a state that helps them solve problems.
principles.apply: Score the pass in the review beside the usability checks.
principles.test: The review contains an aesthetic pass with named criteria.

principles.title: Break the category's norms
principles.rule: Place the concept beside several competitors and name at least two category conventions it breaks on purpose, within what the design system allows.
principles.why: A brand that looks like its category is neither noticed nor remembered.
principles.apply: Default: five competitor references. Use the category's common look as a list of looks to move away from.
principles.test: The notes name two or more deliberately broken category conventions, and a reviewer can pick the concept out of the lineup.

principles.title: Faces and rounded forms for warmth
principles.rule: When the brief asks for warmth or approachability, bring a human presence into the concept, such as a face, character or soft rounded form, checked against the persona.
principles.why: People look for faces and read soft, youthful proportions as trustworthy.
principles.apply: Treat it as a lever, not a rule to make everything cute.
principles.test: An approachable brief's concept includes a human or face-like element that the persona supports.

principles.title: Write a design persona
principles.rule: Write a design persona before visual or copy work: overview, a reference figure, traits, voice, copy samples, a visual lexicon and engagement methods.
principles.why: User personas say who the audience is; the design persona says who the product is.
principles.apply: Ask the user who the product would be if it were a person and build the fields from the answer.
principles.test: A design persona file exists with every field filled.

principles.title: Traits with limits
principles.rule: Give the persona a handful of traits, each paired with the edge it must not cross, plus one trait to avoid entirely.
principles.why: Paired limits such as playful but not childish tell every maker where the edge is.
principles.apply: Default: five to seven traits. Cite a trait for each major visual and copy choice.
principles.test: Every persona trait has a but-not limit and one avoided trait is named.

principles.title: Lexicon gives each choice a trait
principles.rule: Give every palette, typeface and style rule in DESIGN.md a because clause that names the persona trait it expresses.
principles.why: The lexicon makes visual choices carry the same character as the copy.
principles.apply: Reject a visual choice that no trait explains.
principles.test: Each palette, type and style rule in the visual lexicon has a because clause naming a trait.

principles.title: Personality in look, words and behavior
principles.rule: Express the personality through visual design, copy and interaction together on every key screen.
principles.why: A playful look with legal-sounding copy reads as two brands.
principles.apply: Mark one visual, one copy and one interaction detail per key screen that expresses a named trait.
principles.test: Each sampled key screen shows a named trait in all three channels.

principles.title: Tone drops humor as stakes rise
principles.rule: Write copy samples for success, user error and critical failure, and remove humor as severity rises.
principles.why: A brand that jokes during a failure sounds careless.
principles.apply: Keep the samples in the persona and use them as templates for real messages.
principles.test: Side by side, the samples show humor falling and plainness rising with severity.

principles.title: Mascot stays out of the work
principles.rule: Keep any mascot or character out of errors, data readouts, validation and task instructions.
principles.why: A character in the work path slows the task and trivializes the problem.
principles.apply: List each character appearance per flow with its reason.
principles.test: No character appears in error messages, data, form validation or instructions.

principles.title: Clarity beats cleverness
principles.rule: Delete the personality words from each message, and ship the shorter version whenever it is clearer or faster.
principles.why: A joke that needs extra sentences makes the persona too thick.
principles.apply: Never place a joke before the information the user needs.
principles.test: No message gets clearer when its personality words are removed, and no joke precedes needed information.

principles.title: Metaphor tames intimidating subjects
principles.rule: For an abstract or feared subject, name the misconception or fear to overcome and choose a character, metaphor or illustration that disarms it.
principles.why: An imperfect character or a playful machine can make a forbidding subject approachable.
principles.apply: Build the metaphor from the subject itself, not from a stock illustration style.
principles.test: The concept states the fear or misconception it targets and the metaphor chosen for it.

principles.title: Accept who will dislike it
principles.rule: Name who the personality is not for, and do not flatten a design only because it might not appeal to everyone.
principles.why: A clear niche wins more loyal users than it loses.
principles.apply: Answer the might-not-appeal comment with the persona's not-for line.
principles.test: The persona or brief names who the brand is not for.

principles.title: Intent versus impact per feature
principles.rule: For each major feature, write the intended effect, the worst plausible misuse or harm, the group that bears it and the mitigation.
principles.why: Intent and impact differ, and the harm falls on people the team did not picture.
principles.apply: Ask who might be excluded at every review and answer in writing.
principles.test: Each major feature has an intent-versus-impact entry with a mitigation.

principles.title: All-people statements expose exclusion
principles.rule: Write each key assumption as a sentence that starts with all people can, then list the groups for whom it is false and the design response.
principles.why: The phrasing makes excluded groups easy to see.
principles.apply: Run it on interactions that assume sight, speed, money, literacy or a device.
principles.test: Each key interaction has an all-people statement with failing groups and responses.

principles.title: Represent varied people by default
principles.rule: Show varied skin tones, ages, genders, body types and disabilities across human imagery, and build that variety into the system's illustration and avatar parts.
principles.why: Seeing oneself shown creates belonging, and system defaults decide what everyone makes.
principles.apply: Audit every human figure in the deliverable before finalizing.
principles.test: Human imagery does not repeat a single default person across all figures.

principles.title: Fix valleys, place one peak
principles.rule: Map the journey's emotional highs and lows, fix each low with usability or speed and no humor, and place the main peak where a key step closes.
principles.why: The end and the peak of an experience shape the memory of the whole.
principles.apply: Make the last state of each key flow a designed moment rather than a bare confirmation or redirect.
principles.test: Each low step's fix is a usability or speed change, and each key flow ends on a designed state.

principles.title: Surprise rarely, at peaks
principles.rule: Place surprises only at mapped peaks, never in a low moment, and never so often that they become the pattern.
principles.why: Surprise works because it breaks the pattern.
principles.apply: List each surprise element with its journey position.
principles.test: Every surprise sits at a mapped peak and none repeats into a pattern.

principles.title: Story in three beats
principles.rule: Shape any piece meant to be remembered or acted on as tension, turning point and resolution.
principles.why: Stories focus attention and raise recall.
principles.apply: Outline the page, video or infographic in the three beats before layout.
principles.test: The outline has all three beats; a piece missing one is a list, not a story.

principles.title: Admit a limit plainly
principles.rule: State at least one true limitation, open problem or weak result in plain words where the audience is skeptical.
principles.why: Honest admissions are rare, so they stand out and build belief.
principles.apply: Remove every claim on the page that the evidence does not support.
principles.test: The page states at least one real limitation and contains no unsupported claim.

principles.title: Answer fears near the top
principles.rule: List the audience's top fears and answer each near the top of the page in order: the simple fact, the proof, privacy, then technical detail.
principles.why: Answering the fear first turns fear into curiosity.
principles.apply: Take the fear list from research or support messages, not from guesses.
principles.test: Each listed fear has an answer near the top in that order.

principles.title: Plain terms beside the action
principles.rule: State what happens to data, money and safety in plain language next to the action that commits it.
principles.why: Clutter and jargon suggest something is hidden.
principles.apply: Put a one-sentence plain statement beside every consent, payment or data field.
principles.test: Every consent, payment or data request has a plain-language statement next to the action.

principles.title: Calm defaults for volatile data
principles.rule: Choose the default range and first metric of volatile data views to support good long-term decisions, not to look alarming.
principles.why: Short windows on volatile data cause panic and bad choices.
principles.apply: Record the default range and first-read metric with the reason, and keep other ranges available.
principles.test: Each volatile chart records its default range and first metric with a reason.

principles.title: Failure messages are honest updates
principles.rule: Make failure and outage messages say what happened, what is safe, what is being done and when the next update comes, with an apology and no jokes.
principles.why: Regular honest updates show the problem has full attention.
principles.apply: Keep the template in the design system and offer any goodwill gesture only after the facts.
principles.test: The failure template has the four facts, an apology and no humor.

principles.title: Every layer in every slice
principles.rule: Scope each iteration, including the first release, with at least one item for function, reliability, usability and pleasure.
principles.why: Delight promised for after launch rarely ships, and a poor first use is seldom forgiven.
principles.apply: Design exactly one peak moment at the most critical step of a first release.
principles.test: The iteration scope has an item in each of the four layers.

principles.title: Measure each emotional moment
principles.rule: Give each designed peak moment a metric and a baseline before launch, and report the change as a number.
principles.why: Measured results keep emotional design in the plan.
principles.apply: Pick a metric such as support tickets, return visits, mentions or task completion.
principles.test: Each peak moment has a metric with a baseline in the handoff.

principles.title: Confirm the data is relational
principles.rule: Confirm the data holds relationships, or can be converted into them, before committing to a network graph.
principles.why: A network drawing of non-relational data is decoration.
principles.apply: If the relationships are thin, choose another chart through the data-viz skill.
principles.test: The brief names the relationship each edge represents.

principles.title: Several centralities before importance
principles.rule: Call a node important only after more than one centrality measure agrees, and pick the measure that matches the question.
principles.why: Degree, betweenness and closeness answer different questions and can disagree.
principles.apply: Use in-degree and out-degree for directed data and back small degree differences with a second measure.
principles.test: Every claim that a node is important cites at least two measures or a measure matched to the question.

principles.title: Layout never changes the statistics
principles.rule: Read structure from computed statistics, and remember that moving nodes changes only the picture.
principles.why: A layout can make a network look clustered or central when the numbers say otherwise.
principles.apply: Compute the basic structure numbers before styling and compare them with the visual impression.
principles.test: Each structural claim in the caption is backed by a computed statistic.
