principles.title: One purpose per graph
principles.rule: State one purpose for the graph, whether to inform, to persuade, to teach or to delight, for one audience and one story, before touching the data.
principles.why: One purpose drives every later choice of layout, color and size.
principles.apply: Make a separate version when audiences differ instead of serving both in one.
principles.test: The brief holds one purpose sentence naming audience and story.

principles.title: Decide static or interactive first
principles.rule: Choose static or interactive delivery, and where it will be shown, before choosing a layout, and plan annotation up front for static work.
principles.why: The medium sets what the layout must carry on its own.
principles.apply: Default: go interactive early once the network reaches tens of thousands of nodes.
principles.test: The brief names the delivery format and, for static work, the planned title, legend and callouts.

principles.title: Nodes and edges as tables
principles.rule: Model the data as a node table and an edge table, with direction, weight and the grouping and ranking fields stored as data rather than as manual styling.
principles.why: Encodings driven by fields can be recomputed and checked; hand styling cannot.
principles.apply: Keep node attributes in the node table instead of deriving nodes from the edge list.
principles.test: Color, size and group encodings in the graph all trace to named data fields.

principles.title: Bake off several layouts
principles.rule: Test several layouts on the real data before picking one, and never accept the first run.
principles.why: Each layout family reveals different structure, and the first run is rarely the best.
principles.apply: Default: three or four candidates, keeping one render of each with its settings.
principles.test: The record holds renders of several layouts on the real data and the reason for the winner.

principles.title: Layout family follows structure
principles.rule: Pick the layout family from the data and the story: force-directed to discover structure, circular or concentric for a meaningful order or one subject, layered for multipartite data, geographic only when location is the story.
principles.why: A layout that fights the data's shape hides the story.
principles.apply: Use a top-down tree only for directed data with no loops, and avoid 3D unless the third axis encodes something.
principles.test: The decision record ties the chosen layout family to a property of the data or the story.

principles.title: Tune one force at a time
principles.rule: Tune a force layout one setting per iteration, spacing first, keep a render of each step, and stop when an iteration brings no visible gain.
principles.why: Changing several forces at once hides which change helped.
principles.apply: Turn on overlap prevention whenever node sizes vary.
principles.test: The tuning log changes one setting per step with a render each time.

principles.title: A hairball is a defect
principles.rule: Treat an unreadable tangle as a defect to fix with filtering, layering or partitioning, not as a finished result.
principles.why: A graph that shows no story to its own author shows none to anyone.
principles.apply: Keep the layout when patterns exist under clutter and fix spacing and edges first.
principles.test: No published view is an unreadable tangle, and each fix is logged.

principles.title: Edges whisper, nodes speak
principles.rule: Reduce edge visual weight so that edges recede and nodes carry the reading.
principles.why: Edges are the main source of clutter in a network drawing.
principles.apply: Lower edge opacity and width until node groups read clearly at the target size.
principles.test: At the target size, node groups are distinguishable through the edges.

principles.title: Never trade honesty for looks
principles.rule: Style a graph only to make its meaning clearer, and do not publish a view whose structure cannot be shown honestly.
principles.why: Attractive styling that hides or invents relationships misleads.
principles.apply: Improve looks only where the change also makes the graph faster to read.
principles.test: A reviewer finds no styling choice that hides or implies a relationship the data lacks.

principles.title: Classify the structure first
principles.rule: Classify the network as random, hub and spoke, small world or clustered before designing its view.
principles.why: Each structure type has a different story and a different best view.
principles.apply: Mark bridge nodes between clusters when the story is about flow, adoption or risk.
principles.test: The design notes name the structure type and the evidence for it.

principles.title: Spread rules beside spread graphics
principles.rule: Show change over time as snapshots that share one layout and one legend, and state the spread rule and time step next to them.
principles.why: Without a fixed layout and a stated rule, the viewer cannot read what changed or why.
principles.apply: Use the same node positions in every snapshot.
principles.test: Every spread graphic states its rule and time step and every snapshot shares one layout.

principles.title: Say what was filtered out
principles.rule: Tell the viewer what a filter removed, and recompute statistics on the filtered subgraph when a claim is about it.
principles.why: A filtered view presented as the whole network misleads.
principles.apply: Put the filter and its cut-off in the caption; call any threshold a judgment.
principles.test: Every filtered view states its filter in the caption.

principles.title: Several small views beat one
principles.rule: Prefer several small filtered views, such as an ego network, the most connected nodes and in-group versus cross-group edges, over one view of everything.
principles.why: Each small view answers one question clearly.
principles.apply: Explore with single filters before combining them, and set ego depth on purpose.
principles.test: The deliverable answers its questions with focused views rather than one dense overview alone.

principles.title: Components before distance measures
principles.rule: Count connected components and report the giant component's share before running distance measures or reading the picture as one network.
principles.why: Path statistics on a broken network are meaningless.
principles.apply: Run statistics in three tiers: whole network, node centrality, then clustering.
principles.test: Any reported diameter or path length follows a stated component count.

principles.title: State every score's direction
principles.rule: Write down the direction of every score before mapping it, and run a numeric ramp from light for low to dark for high.
principles.why: A reader who cannot tell whether dark means more misreads the whole graph.
principles.apply: Put the direction in the legend.
principles.test: Each numeric encoding's legend states which end is high.

principles.title: Segment by data type
principles.rule: Encode a categorical attribute with distinct colors, a numeric attribute with size or a ramp, and use an algorithmic clustering only when no attribute fits.
principles.why: The encoding must match the kind of value it shows.
principles.apply: Default: two to about fifteen categorical colors; reset to a neutral baseline before each new encoding.
principles.test: Every encoding in the graph matches the type of its source field.

source.part: Chapter 7: Segmenting and partitioning a graph

principles.title: Scale area, not radius
principles.rule: Scale node area to the data value, give the smallest node a visible size and cap the largest so it does not hide its neighbors.
principles.why: Area grows with the square of the radius, so scaling the radius exaggerates differences.
principles.apply: Label an exaggerated size range when it survives into a deliverable.
principles.test: Node sizes are proportional to value by area, with a visible minimum and a cap.

source.part: Chapter 7: Segmenting and partitioning a graph

principles.title: Highlight one group, gray the rest
principles.rule: Direct attention to the story subset by changing two channels, such as color and size, for that group and leaving every other node neutral.
principles.why: One distinct highlight reads instantly; several compete.
principles.apply: Reserve one highlight color for the story and keep it out of the category palette.
principles.test: Only the story subset carries the highlight, and the rest of the graph is neutral.

source.part: Chapter 7: Segmenting and partitioning a graph

principles.title: Clusterings are one reading
principles.rule: Run a clustering at several settings, reject over- and under-segmented results, and present the chosen one as one reading with its method in the caption.
principles.why: Default settings and single runs produce arbitrary groups.
principles.apply: Validate clusters by eye against the layout and against a known attribute.
principles.test: The caption names the clustering method, and the record shows several settings compared.

source.part: Chapter 7: Segmenting and partitioning a graph

principles.title: Time only when it changes
principles.rule: Add a time dimension only when the network changes often within the period shown, and fix node positions before comparing steps.
principles.why: A timeline over a static network adds controls and no story.
principles.apply: Map change in stature to size, status to color and tie strength to edge width.
principles.test: A dynamic graph shows visible change between steps and keeps node positions fixed.

principles.title: Gaps stay visible
principles.rule: Gray out periods with no observations instead of dropping them or plotting them as real values.
principles.why: Hidden gaps read as stability or as zero.
principles.apply: Say whether the view is instantaneous or cumulative.
principles.test: Periods with no data are marked as gaps in every time view.

principles.title: Legend says node, edge, color
principles.rule: State in every network legend what a node is, what an edge means and what color encodes, and give the graph a title, credit and short description.
principles.why: A network without these three answers cannot be read.
principles.apply: Add an about view with sources, objective and metrics to interactive graphs.
principles.test: Every published network graph names its node, edge and color meanings and has a title.

source.part: Chapter 9: Taking your graph beyond Gephi

principles.title: Interactive graphs focus on demand
principles.rule: On hover or select, dim everything except the node and its neighbors, reveal labels by zoom level, and provide search when the network is large.
principles.why: Focus on demand keeps a large network readable.
principles.apply: Hold the interactive view to the same clarity standard as a static one.
principles.test: Selecting a node dims non-neighbors and labels appear in order of importance as the viewer zooms.

source.part: Chapter 9: Taking your graph beyond Gephi

principles.title: Vector master for print
principles.rule: Keep a vector master of any network that will be edited, annotated or printed, and finish static versions with title, callouts and labels outside the graph tool.
principles.why: Raster exports cannot be cleanly annotated or scaled.
principles.apply: Use a light background for print and allow dark only on screen.
principles.test: A vector master exists for each printed or edited network graph.

source.part: Chapter 9: Taking your graph beyond Gephi

principles.title: Static graph carries whole story
principles.rule: Make a static network deliverable carry the full story through snapshots, supporting statistics, a narrative and callouts.
principles.why: A static reader cannot click for the missing context.
principles.apply: Take snapshots at boundaries that mean something in the domain and put trend charts as small multiples on one shared axis.
principles.test: The static deliverable includes snapshots, statistics, narrative and callouts.

principles.title: Name the AI app archetype
principles.rule: Before designing, classify the product as an AI app or not and, if it is one, name its archetype: assistant with memory, autonomous agent or real-time prediction system.
principles.why: The archetype decides which runtime states the interface must design for.
principles.apply: Record the archetype in the brief and let it select the state list the screens must cover.
principles.test: The brief of an AI product names its archetype.

principles.title: Memory the user can see
principles.rule: Design an AI product so the end user never repeats a standing instruction and can see and edit what it remembers about them.
principles.why: Remembered preferences feel helpful only when they are visible and correctable.
principles.apply: Add a memory view to the screen inventory with edit and delete controls.
principles.test: The design includes a place to view and change stored preferences.

principles.title: Design fast and slow answers
principles.rule: Design two answer speeds, near-instant and slow, and mark which answers must never be reused from a cache.
principles.why: Reused answers arrive at once while new ones take time, and stale reuse is wrong for live facts.
principles.apply: Give the slow path a visible progress state and the fast path no fake delay.
principles.test: The state sheet shows both speeds and lists the answer types that bypass reuse.

source.part: Step 2: Speed up responses with semantic caching

principles.title: Vendor numbers are claims
principles.rule: Treat performance and cost figures from a vendor document as claims until the project measures its own.
principles.why: Self-reported figures for one product come with no method.
principles.apply: Write such figures into notes as vendor-reported and keep them out of gates.
principles.test: No gate or decision cites a vendor figure without a project measurement.

source.part: Step 2: Speed up responses with semantic caching

principles.title: Route by task, not habit
principles.rule: Route each request to the best-fit resource, such as a general model, a specialized model, search or an outside service, from a catalog with use-when lines.
principles.why: Habitual routing sends work to a tool that is worse at it.
principles.apply: Apply the same rule to design tools: pick from the tool catalog by capability.
principles.test: Each routed tool call in the plan cites the catalog's use-when line it matches.

principles.title: Rate limits are a designed state
principles.rule: Design the usage-limit message as a first-class state that says what happened, when access returns and, for tiered plans, the remaining allowance.
principles.why: An unexplained refusal reads as a broken product.
principles.apply: Include the limited state in every AI interaction's state sheet.
principles.test: Every AI interaction has a designed limited state with recovery information.

source.part: Step 4: Keep your app safe with rate limiting

principles.title: Show how fresh numbers are
principles.rule: Show the age of every live or predicted number on a real-time dashboard.
principles.why: A stale number presented as current leads to wrong decisions.
principles.apply: Add a freshness label or timestamp to each live metric in the layout.
principles.test: Each live metric on the dashboard shows its freshness.

source.part: Step 5: Speed up ML predictions with a feature store

principles.title: Hand off runtime behavior
principles.rule: Hand off an AI interaction with a runtime-behavior sheet covering waiting, fast answer, slow answer, limited and failed or fallback states, not only screens.
principles.why: Static screens omit the states that decide whether an AI product feels reliable.
principles.apply: Split ownership: design owns states, copy and visible behavior; code owns storage, thresholds and enforcement.
principles.test: The handoff for each AI interaction lists all five states with designed screens or copy.

source.part: Final thoughts and what to build next

principles.title: Record tools, layer and transport
principles.rule: Record each connector's layer, its transport and the tools it exposes, not only its name.
principles.why: The connector name says little about what a workflow can call.
principles.apply: Fill these fields in the tool catalog entry before routing design work to the connector.
principles.test: Each catalog entry lists layer, transport and exposed tools.

principles.title: Read the live connector list
principles.rule: Read the host's live list of connectors before planning a workflow, and never assume a connector is present.
principles.why: Plans built on an absent tool fail midway.
principles.apply: When a needed connector is missing, tell the user which one and why, then continue with the catalog fallback.
principles.test: The plan cites a live check of each connector it relies on.

principles.title: Check write access first
principles.rule: Check whether a connector can write before designing a workflow that needs it to write.
principles.why: A workflow designed around a write the tool cannot perform dead-ends.
principles.apply: Map a write-capable connector or change the plan when the default one is read-only.
principles.test: Every workflow step that writes uses a connector recorded as write-capable.

principles.title: Try local, then promote
principles.rule: Add a new connector at the narrowest scope first and promote it to project or user scope only after it passes verification.
principles.why: A broken shared connector breaks every session that loads it.
principles.apply: Back up or version the configuration before editing it.
principles.test: Newly added connectors start at local scope with a recorded verification before promotion.

principles.title: Connected means a real call
principles.rule: Mark a connector connected only after a real tool call succeeds, not when it appears in a list.
principles.why: Listed servers can still fail on authorization or schema.
principles.apply: Restart the host after a configuration change, then make one read-only call.
principles.test: Each connector marked connected has a recorded successful call.

principles.title: Secrets live outside config
principles.rule: Pass secrets to a local server as environment variables and never write a secret into a command, a committed config or the catalog.
principles.why: Committed secrets leak to everyone who reads the repository.
principles.apply: Limit a file-access server to the narrowest folder the task needs.
principles.test: No command, committed config or catalog entry contains a secret value.

principles.title: Build only when none exists
principles.rule: Build a new connector only when no existing one covers the capability, and hand the build to the coding side while design registers the result.
principles.why: Building duplicates what the directory already offers and spreads maintenance.
principles.apply: Search built-in, then directory, then custom options in that order before proposing a build.
principles.test: A proposed connector build cites the search of existing options that found none.
